The Mystery of #Thursday #Praise of the Virgin Mary

Brethren, today we behold the fourth day of thanksgiving, the fifth day of creation a day on which the heavens are illumined with the light of the Queen of Heaven, our Lady, the Theotokos. On this day the throne of light is adorned, and the saints, prophets, and apostles gather more abundantly, for she, the Mother of God, has entered to bless and to intercede.

As Moses beheld the bush in the wilderness that burned yet was not consumed (Exod. 3:1-4), so we behold the mystery of Mary: in her womb dwelt the Fire of Divinity, yet her virginity was not consumed. Just as the divine nature of Christ remained unchanged in taking flesh, so the bush remained green in the midst of flame. He who is God by nature became man without ceasing to be what He was; through this union, salvation has visited us. Therefore, let us cry: “O Lady, pray for us, that we may not lose the grace and glory of Your Son, who became man for our salvation.”

Mary as the New Eve

Eve, through disobedience, closed the gate of Eden, and the cherubim with the flaming sword stood guard (Gen. 3:24). But Mary, through obedience, opened it again.
Saint James the Apostle teaches: The day of Adam’s death was changed into a day of life; the serpent’s deceit was replaced by Gabriel’s truth; Eve’s fall was reversed by Mary’s acceptance of the divine Word. What was torn down in Eden was rebuilt on earth by the Virgin. Where the serpent sowed lies, Gabriel spoke truth, loosing the bonds of death. The very door through which death entered became the door through which life returned.

The devil begot Cain the bringer of death through Eve’s deception; but through Mary’s conception by the Holy Spirit came the Living Word, who brought eternal life. In Eden Adam was cast out into exile; on Calvary, through the Cross of Mary’s Son, the thief entered again into Paradise with his forefather Adam. The poisoned counsel of the serpent was answered by the honeyed counsel of the Archangel. Through Mary’s “Yes,” the tower of deceit was demolished, and the Tree of Life Christ’s Body and Blood was offered to the faithful.

The Joy and Dignity of Her Motherhood

What greater joy could a woman know than to bear a child? Yet Mary’s joy surpassed all, for she bore God Himself. The angel declared: “You shall bear a son and call His name Emmanuel” (Matt. 1:20–21). which being interpreted is, God with us. With out sin he become one with us .to save His people from their sins. If He were only God, He could not suffer; if He were only man, He could not save. In the Virgin’s womb both were united without confusion, for the salvation of the world.

Saint John Chrysostom warns us not to profane so great a gift: If we, once children of wrath, have been made children of grace through such a birth, how much greater will be our punishment if we live unworthily!

The Magi’s gifts speak to the mystery:

Gold for His kingship, reflecting the purity of those who believe in Him.

Frankincense for His divinity, pure as faith and conduct must be.

Myrrh for His death, healing what was broken, uniting what was divided, restoring Adam to communion with the angels.

The Mystery of the Second Creation

From Adam’s side came Eve; from a Virgin’s womb came Christ. In this, the Creator was born of His creature, and He who made His mother was nourished at her breast. The flesh He formed from nothing He now takes as His own. This is a mystery beyond the grasp of the senses seen only through the eyes of faith.

Therefore, let us constantly call upon her intercession, for she is the good among the saints, the chosen vessel of the Incarnation. The apostles themselves magnified her, knowing the abundance of grace poured upon the world through her Son’s humanity.

The Prophets Foretell Her Son

God swore to David that from his line would come the One who would sit upon his throne (Ps. 131:1). Bethlehem, the “house of bread,” was chosen as His birthplace (Mic. 5:2; John 6:51). Saint Jerome hails it: “O house of bread, from you is born the Bread that came down from heaven.” From here the Shepherd of Israel would arise, the One whose goings forth are from everlasting.

The Water of Bethlehem and the Martyrs’ Example

When David longed for water from Bethlehem’s well (2 Sam. 23:15–17), his warriors risked their lives to bring it. David, seeing the price they had paid, poured it out before the Lord it was their blood. So too, the martyrs despised the sweetness of this world and shed their blood for God. As David poured out the water for God’s glory, so the saints poured out their lives, and we are called to follow their steadfastness in the spiritual battle.

The Humility of the Incarnation

He who saw humanity crushed under the serpent’s heel humbled Himself to take our nature not that of angels but flesh from the Virgin’s womb (Isa. 59:6; Heb. 4:14). Born in Bethlehem, He redeemed us by His blood (Eph. 1:7), drawing near to us who were once far from the covenant (Eph. 2:11–13).

Thus, brethren, let us praise the Virgin, the Cross, and her divine Son. Let us beseech her purity and holiness to keep us from losing the grace and glory purchased by Christ.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

“The Mystery of #Tears in #Prayer:

A Holy Offering of the Penitent Heart

(Part 4)

Beloved brethren in Christ, children of the holy Church, today let us lift up our minds to consider with reverence the mystery of prayer with tears. For this is not a light matter, nor a fleeting emotion, but a holy labor of the soul an offering more precious than gold, more fragrant than incense, more powerful than eloquent words. To pray with tears is to pour out before the Lord not merely words,nothing is required but a contrite heart, and no one can hinder a soul from drawing near to Him. as David the Prophet has proclaimed: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O Lord, Thou wilt not despise” (Psalm 50:17).

The Essence of True Prayer

The Lord Himself has taught us that God does not incline His ear to the ornament of speech nor to the many words that tumble from our lips, but to the hidden purity of the spirit (Matt. 6:7–8). For even before we ask, He knows what we need, since nothing is hidden from His eyes. What then is prayer with tears? It is not the raising of a loud voice, nor the weaving of elegant phrases, but the trembling of the soul before its Creator, the melting of the heart as wax before the fire, the sigh of the sinner who knows his own unworthiness yet dares to hope in divine mercy.

Tears in prayer are the sign of the heart’s breaking open before God. , and the wordless plea which God cannot despise. For the Almighty says, “I am a God who is near, not a God who is far off” (Jer. 23:23). If He is near, then what hinders us? Not our lack of eloquence, not our unlearned speech, not the absence of a mediator, nor the cold refusal of a king’s court. No our distance comes only from the hardness of our own hearts. The moment you draw near with humility, God draws near to you.

The Posture of the Soul in Prayer

What then must accompany such prayer?

A humble heart and a broken spirit.

Tears not for the perishing glories of this world, but for the everlasting kingdom.

Requests not for wrath upon our enemies, nor for worldly revenge, but for the virtues of the Spirit.

The banishment of grudges, anger, and violence from the soul.

A tongue that speaks well of others, never poisoning the air with malice.

A life that shuns the company of the wicked and refuses fellowship with the devil, the enemy of mankind.

For many pray deceitfully, repeating the words “Forgive us, as we forgive” (Matt. 6:12) while harboring bitterness in their hearts. Such prayers are empty echoes, rising no higher than the ceiling above them.

The Nearness of God in Prayer

When you say, “Our Father, who art in heaven,” do not imagine that God is far off, enthroned in unreachable heights. Rather, in prayer your heart ascends, and you become heavenly, one with the Father above. In that moment you stand before the Lord of all creation, before Him at Whose voice heaven and earth tremble. Therefore, let no one think lightly of prayer, for to pray is to enter the throne room of the Almighty.

The Fruit of Prayer with Tears

David exhorts us: “Taste and see that the Lord is good” (Ps. 34:8). Prayer with tears is the tasting of that goodness. He who prays with tears knows by experience the sweetness of divine mercy. He understands that even if his requests are delayed, but because the Father of lights gives only what is good and in due season (Matt. 7:11). Many times we ask for what would harm us, and if God granted all our requests, we would perish by our own folly. Therefore, true prayer with tears does not cling to its own will but entrusts itself to the divine will, saying: “Not as I will, but as Thou wilt” (Matt. 26:39).

The Fire of Love in Prayer

Prayer is the flame of love between man and God. The one who loves does not tire of conversation with his beloved. Even if night falls and day rises again, still he lingers in the presence of his Friend. So it was with the saints: their minds were always bound to God, whether in solitude or among crowds. In silence they conversed with Him; in company they remembered Him.

Their hearts burned like a hidden censer, unceasingly rising in prayer as naturally as breath itself. Thus did Saint Gregory teach us: that a Christian ought to think of God even more than he breathes.

Conclusion

Beloved brethren, to pray with tears is to let the soul itself become a sacrifice, poured out in humility before the God who is near. It is to cast aside pride, anger, and earthly desires, and to taste the sweetness of His goodness. It is to live as one who always longs for God, never tiring of His presence, never weary of His love. Let us then learn to pray in this way, not with empty words, but with broken hearts, with tears of repentance, with trust in His will. For such prayer pierces the heavens and brings down mercy upon us.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.

The Feast of the #Ascension of Our #Lady (Nehase 16)

Beloved brethren in Christ, children of the Holy Church, today we gather to contemplate with awe and reverence the radiant mystery of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the Ark of the New Covenant, whom the Orthodox Tewahedo Church solemnly commemorates on the 16th of Nehase. With holy fear and joy let us ascend in thought and devotion, that we may stand mystically among the apostles, the angels, and all the heavenly hosts who witnessed her translation into glory.

The Life of the Theotokos

The days of her earthly sojourn were sixty-four years.

She dwelt in her mother’s house for three years.

She consecrated her youth in the Temple for twelve years.

In Joseph’s house she conceived the Lord for nine months and five days.

She remained with her divine Son for thirty-three years and three months.

When the hour of the Cross came, the Lord, our Redeemer, entrusted His most pure Mother to His beloved disciple John, saying: “Behold, your mother” (Jn. 19:26–27). At that hour He made us all her children, granting her as our Mother and advocate forever.

Her Union with the Apostles and the Descent of the Holy Spirit

After the Ascension of Christ, she remained with the apostles in prayer (Acts 1:14). the Holy Spirit descended and filled the Apostols with tongues of fire and the gift of seventy-two languages. For fifteen years John cherished her as his mother, as the Lord Himself had commanded.

The Call to Glory

When she reached the age of sixty-four, her Son appeared and said to her: “I will take you from this world to the heavenly dwelling that shall not pass away.”the apostles, who wept, saying: Our Lady, where are you going?” She replied: “ My Son has called me.”

She told them that the time had come for her to depart to that eternal world. When the apostles heard this, they were deeply grieved and wept bitterly.

At that moment, holy angels appeared and comforted the apostles, saying to them, “Do not grieve and do not weep, but rejoice and accompany her with joy.”

The Promise of Her Son

The Lord said to His Mother, “Blessed are the breasts that nourished Me, for I am the Provider of all creation. I will take you to the heavenly heights and feed you with the good things of My Father.
,you placed Me upon your lap, O Virgin Mother Mary, and I will take you with Me to heaven and to My good Father, setting you upon the chariot of the cherubim.”

Thus He prepared to receive His Mother as the Queen arrayed in splendor.

Her Dormition

On a Sunday, her soul, pure as snow, was taken into the hands of her Son amid the company of angels. Christ Himself received her soul and entrusted it to the Archangel Michael. Saint Yared, the Ethiopian melodist, sang: “Your love is pure, O Mother of God; your Son has called you to eternal life.”

The apostles reverently honored her body, wrapping it in a shroud and burying it with hymns and praises, while angels filled the air with fragrance.

The Envy of the Jews

But the adversary stirred envy among the Jews. As they sought to profane her body, the angel Gabriel struck down Taufania, who dared to touch her bier. Saint John, unwilling to be separated from her, declared: “I will not abandon my trust; I will die with her.” Then, in glory, Michael and Gabriel took her body and John in a cloud and placed them in Paradise under the Tree of Life.

Her Glorious Resurrection and Ascension

On the sixteenth of Nehase, her Son commanded: “My Mother, arise and come to Me.” At His word, her soul and body were reunited, and she rose in glory. Angels filled the heavens, David sang: “At Your right hand stands the queen in gold” (Ps. 44:9), and the whole creation was filled with fragrance.

Saints Tsige Dengel and Gebre Mariam testify in Mahlete Tsige that the Virgin’s glory exceeded that of the world, and that she was carried by angels with hymns sweeter than incense. Saint Yared too sang: “Mary was taken up in glory, and the angels and archangels came to receive her.”


Saints Tsige Dengel and Gebre Mariam testify in Mahlete Tsige that the Virgin’s glory exceeded that of the world, and that she was carried by angels with hymns sweeter than incense. Saint Yared too sang: “Mary was taken up in glory, and the angels and archangels came to receive her.”

Even the apostle Thomas, arriving late, beheld her being borne upward in splendor. When he told the others, they opened her tomb and found it empty, Then he showed them the girdle (belt) of Mary, which she had given him as a sign. And the apostles, seeing this miracle, fell down in worship, glorifying God for the bodily assumption of the Ever-Virgin Mary into paradise. For this reason, the Church venerates the holy girdle(Seben) as a memorial of her translation.

Scriptural Prophecies Fulfilled

The prophets foretold her glory:

“Arise, O Lord, into Your resting place, You and the Ark of Your strength” (Ps. 131:8).

“Who is this that comes up from the wilderness like pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense?” (Song of Songs 3:6).

“At Your right hand stands the queen arrayed in gold” (Ps. 44:9).

Saint John the Theologian bore witness: “The temple of God was opened in heaven, and the ark of His covenant was seen” (Rev. 11:19). He also saw “a woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars” (Rev. 12:1).

Thus the Scriptures proclaim that the Virgin, untouched by corruption and sin, was raised by her Son in glory. As death entered by Eve, so life and incorruption were revealed in Mary, the new Eve.

Conclusion

Therefore, beloved, let us lift our hearts in thanksgiving. For today we celebrate the mystery of mysteries the Assumption of our Lady, the Mother of God. She who bore the Lord of Glory now intercedes for us at His right hand. Let us rejoice, not as those who mourn, but as those who have gained a Mother in heaven, radiant and powerful, the refuge of sinners, the joy of the righteous, the Queen clothed

What Does #Covenant #Mercy Mean?

Dear followers of the Orthodox faith, peace and greetings in the name of our Lord. Today, we present to you a teaching on the mystery of Covenant Mercy, that you may read it, learn from it, and be strengthened in faith.

The Meaning of Covenant

The word covenant is derived from the Gəʿəz verb that means to make a covenant, to swear an oath, to make a promise. This word is often used in the Holy Scriptures.

“These are the words of the covenant” (Deut. 29:1).

“I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel” (Jer. 31:31–33).

“I have made a covenant with my chosen one” (Ps. 88:3).

Covenant of Mercy

The Covenant of Mercy (Kidane Mehret) means the oath of mercy. It is one of the thirty-three feasts of the Virgin Mary celebrated by the Church.

After the resurrection, when our Lady was leaving the tomb of the Lord, she asked Him in prayer:

“My beloved Son, You took flesh from me, You dwelt in my womb for nine months and five days, and I followed You in all Your journeys. I beg You to hear my prayer.”

At that moment, the tomb shook and was split open. The Lord appeared with ten thousand angels and said to her:

“Peace be to you, Mary. What do you ask Me to do for you?”

And she replied:

Whoever celebrates my memorial,

Whoever has compassion on the poor in my name,

Whoever builds a church in my name,

Whoever gives alms for my sake,

Whoever names his son after me with faith and love save them, O Lord, from death of body and soul.

The Lord then promised her, saying: “My covenant is with you, O my Mother, in the name of the living God, in the Holy Spirit.”

The Covenant in Scripture

The word covenant is mentioned in the Old Testament about 280 times, often in connection with the word word. In the New Testament, it appears more than thirty-three times.

The word mercy also comes from the Gəʿəz tongue, meaning forgiveness, compassion, agreement, oath. A covenant of mercy, therefore, is firmer and weightier than any human contract.

God’s Covenant with His Saints

As the Psalmist says: “I have made a covenant with my chosen ones” (Ps. 88:3). God has made covenants with His saints and continues to do so. His covenant is always a covenant of mercy.

The writings of the holy fathers, mothers, and martyrs tell us that before their death, God often revealed Himself to them and gave them this covenant of mercy.

This covenant is not limited to their souls alone, but extends even to:

their names,

their crosses,

their clothing,

the books that recorded their deaths,

the soil they walked upon,

and the places where they struggled.

For this reason, we venerate holy places, for God has made covenants through them.

God Reveals the Time of Death

It is not unusual in the Holy Scriptures for God to reveal the time and manner of a saint’s death.

Christ told Peter the way he would die (Jn. 21:19; 2 Pet. 1:14).

Paul was told about his departure (Acts 20:25; 21:10).

“I will appear to him before his death” is also written (Sene Golgotha).

God does this not for the saints’ own benefit, but so that those who come after may be strengthened. The saints themselves have already finished their race, but through their covenant of mercy, we receive encouragement and salvation.

Why the Covenant of Mercy Is Necessary

Why is the covenant of mercy needed? Because where there is sin, there must also be punishment, as seen from Adam. Mankind bears this responsibility, and without God’s mercy, no one could stand.

Therefore, God provided many ways for salvation, one of which is the covenant of mercy. Every covenant of mercy calls us to good works.

There is no covenant without obligation. God promises mercy to:

those who call upon His name,

those who remember the saints,

those who feed the hungry,

those who clothe the naked,

those who welcome the stranger,

those who read and hear the Scriptures,

those who give alms.

To all such, He says: “I will forgive their sins; I will pardon them.”

Thus, the covenant of mercy does not lead us to laziness, but to action. Even if we cannot do the greatest deeds, we can do the smallest, and God, in His compassion, accepts them.

The Greatness of God’s Goodness

The goodness of God surpasses all understanding. Many saints were promised mercy “until the end of time.”

Gabriel the Archangel was chosen to announce the mystery of salvation (Lk. 1:19–26).

Queen Esther overturned the decree of death for her people (Esth. 3:10).

Moses interceded for Israel, saying: “Forgive their sin, but if not, blot me out of Your book” (Ex. 32:32).

In all these, we see that God grants mercy not for the saints alone, but for the whole human race.

The Virgin Mary as the Covenant of Mercy

Above all covenants, the greatest was given to the Virgin Mary. For she is not only chosen, but chosen above all the chosen. She is superior in holiness to every saint.

Therefore, the covenant of mercy given to her is greater than all others. For this reason, she is herself called “The Covenant of Mercy.”

The eyes of every sinner look with hope to her covenant, for in her intercession lies the medicine of salvation, given by her Son for the freedom of mankind.

Conclusion

Beloved brethren, let us remember always the greatness of the Covenant of Mercy. Through it, God calls us to repentance, to good works, and to hope. Let us never despair of salvation, but with faith in Christ and with the intercession of His Mother, let us walk the path of righteousness until the end.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

5058:
“Has Our #Lady, the Holy #Virgin #Mary, Been Taken to Heaven?”


Beloved children of the Holy Church, peace be to you in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Today we reflect on the great mystery of the Ascension of Our Lady, the Holy Virgin Mary, who was taken up into heaven with glory and honor, beyond all creatures visible and invisible.

The Appearance of Mary in Paradise

When the time came for our Lady, the Holy Virgin Mary, to depart from this earthly life, the holy apostles were deeply grieved, for they loved her as their mother. Yet our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ did not leave them comfortless.

One day, He appeared to them, assuring them that they would behold His Mother once more. At that time, Saint John the Evangelist, who was preaching in Asia, was carried away by the Holy Spirit and transported to paradise.

There, under the Tree of Life, he saw our Lord Jesus Christ seated in majesty. Beside Him was the holy body of His pure Mother. “He commanded the seven archangels to summon the earth to release the body of the pure Mother of God. The holy angels obeyed His word, and at that moment, the body of Our Lady, the Holy Virgin Mary, emerged from the tomb beneath the Tree of Life.”

Then our Lord spoke tenderly to her, saying: “O my beloved Mother, who bore Me in the flesh, come, ascend with Me into the eternal kingdom of heaven.” At that moment, all the plants of paradise bowed in reverence, the angels and martyrs praised her, and with unspeakable joy, they escorted her into the heavenly heights.

Saint John received a blessing from her, worshipped, and returned to the earth, bearing witness of what he had seen.

The Apostles’ Grief and Christ’s Consolation

When John returned, he found the apostles still mourning. He told them of the glory he had witnessed, but they sorrowed because they had not seen it with their own eyes. While they wept, Christ Himself appeared among them, saying: “Peace be with you. Why do you grieve for the body of My Mother Mary? Behold, I have shown her glory. Rejoice in your hearts!” Then He ascended again into heaven.

The apostles, comforted, continued steadfast in prayer.

The Apostles’ Fast and the Heavenly Vision

As the month of Nehase began, Saint John said: “Let us fast and pray these two weeks, that our Lord Jesus Christ may grant us to behold the body of His Mother in glory.”

Thus, the apostles fasted from the first of Nehase until the sixteenth. On that day, our Lord appeared again, taking them up into heaven, where they beheld the Holy Virgin seated at the right hand of her beloved Son. She stretched forth her hands, blessed them, and filled them with joy.

At that time, our Lord celebrated the holy Mysteries of His Body and Blood, assisted by Saint Stephen the Archdeacon. When the Eucharist was offered, great and unending joy filled heaven and earth.

Then Christ spoke to His Mother, saying: “I command My apostles to proclaim throughout the world the memorial of your Ascension on this day. Whoever honors you and partakes of My Body and Blood shall not see the torment of fire. I grant forgiveness of sins to those who remember you and who show mercy to the poor on this day.”

Hearing this, Our Lady glorified God and blessed the apostles.

Her Resting and Translation

After her repose in the flesh, the apostles prepared to bury her body. Yet because of the malice of the Jews, our Lord bestowed another glory upon her: her body was carried from Gethsemane and placed in Paradise under the Tree of Life for two hundred and five days, until the sixteenth of Nehase.

Just as Christ, by His divine power, rose from the dead, so too did His Mother share in the victory of resurrection. Thus was fulfilled the prophecy of the Song of Songs: “Arise, my beloved, my beautiful one, and come away; for behold, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone. The flowers appear on the earth, the time of singing has come” (Song 2:10–12).

All her earthly sufferings the exile in Egypt, the hunger and thirst, the anguish at the Cross when the sword pierced her soul were transformed into eternal joy.

The Glory of the Resurrection of Our Lady

Now she no longer beholds her Son crucified but glorified. She no longer weeps in sorrow but rejoices in the eternal kingdom, where there is no pain, no death, no separation. She has entered into the place where the saints receive their crowns, where she reigns in glory above all creation.

Among the thirty-three feasts of Our Lady, the most exalted is the 16th of Nehase, the day of her holy Ascension. From the 17th to the 21st of Nehase, her resurrection is celebrated for five days, just as we celebrate the Resurrection of her Son for fifty days.

Nehase 18 – Memorial of her Resurrection

Nehase 19 – Memorial of her Resurrection

Nehase 20 – Memorial of her Resurrection

Nehase 21 – Memorial of her Resurrection

Exhortation to the Faithful

Beloved children of God, let us therefore honor the Mother of our Lord with joy and purity of heart. She is our intercessor, our refuge, and our hope before the throne of her Son. Whoever remembers her with faith shall obtain mercy, forgiveness, and blessing.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.

Can We Deliver #Prayer to Our #Home?

(Part 5)

Beloved friends in Christ who follow the Orthodox teachings, we greet you with the peace of God. Today, on this blessed subject, we present a teaching for your benefit, that you may read, meditate, and grow in the life of prayer.

The Example of the Hermits

The hermits who dwell in deserts and caves, separating themselves from the noise of the world, continually lift up prayers for the salvation of mankind. Though they live apart, they return to the monasteries to receive the Body and Blood of our Lord, for without the Eucharist no soul can live. Their life teaches us that prayer can be offered in every place, yet the Holy Mysteries are essential for eternal life.

Prayer in the Home

Christians who live among the gentile , where there is no church nearby, should not neglect their worship of God. They must offer prayer and thanksgiving in their homes. In this regard, the ancient Egyptian Christians gave us a shining example: in each of their houses they prepared a place for prayer. When they went to the church for the Divine Liturgy, they never returned without partaking of the Body and Blood of the Lord except for some special reason.

Likewise, they strove to keep the seven hours of prayer wherever they were. In this discipline, even those outside the Church put many of us to shame, they have better experience than us . For we see that infidels and heretics will not fail to perform their appointed hours of worship whether at home, at school, at work, in the market, or even on the road. How much of us, who worship the true God, faithful to the rule of prayer handed down by our Fathers?

A Call to Examine Ourselves

Let each of us ask with sincerity:

Have I prepared a place of prayer in my home?

Do I gather my family for prayer when I cannot attend the church?

Do I strive to keep the seven prayer hours where I am?

Do I make prayer a daily habit, not only in the church but in every place and time?

For prayer is not bound by walls; it is the incense of the soul that rises to heaven from every faithful heart.

The Command to Pray Seven Times a Day

Our Holy Church has ordained that we should pray seven times daily, following the testimony of Scripture:

“Seven times a day I will praise You for Your righteous judgments.” (Psalm 118:164)

Just as the holy Prophet David glorified God seven times a day, so also we, walking in the footsteps of our Fathers and according to the canons of the Church, must offer prayer at the appointed hours.

The Seven Times of Prayer

1. Morning Prayer – As David said, “My God, my God, early will I seek You” (Psalm 62:1). When the night ends and the light of day dawns, we rise from our beds and give thanks to God who preserved us through the night.

It was in the morning that Adam was created (Gen. 1:26).

It was in the morning that our Lord Jesus Christ was examined before Pilate (Matt. 27:1).

It is the hour when the angel of the night departs and the angel of the day takes his place.

2. The Third Hour (3:00 am )– At this time:

Eve was created as a helper for Adam (Gen. 2:21–24).

Daniel prayed with his face toward Jerusalem (Dan. 6:10).

The Archangel Gabriel announced the good news to the Virgin Mary (Luke 1:26).

Christ was scourged before Pilate (Matt. 27:26).

The Holy Spirit descended upon the Apostles (Acts 2:1–4).
Thus, at this hour we give thanks for the gift of creation, salvation, and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit.

3. Midday Prayer (Noon) – When the sun burns hot, our bodies grow weary, our minds are scattered, and the demons press upon us. For this reason, we strengthen ourselves and cry to God (Psalm 54:17).

At this hour Adam ate of the forbidden tree and fell from glory (Gen. 3:6).

At this hour Enoch built the altar to the Lord (cf. Gen. 5:22).

Above all, it was at this hour that our Lord Jesus Christ was nailed to the Cross for our salvation (John 19:14).

Therefore, we pray that we may not fall into temptation but be strengthened by the Crucified One.
(and the remaining hours continue likewise, each filled with meaning and mystery Midafternoon, Evening, Sunset, and Midnight prayers all reminding us of God’s mighty works in creation and salvation.)

Conclusion

Beloved, prayer is the breath of the soul. If the righteous of old kept vigil and offered their hearts to God seven times daily, how much more should we, who have received the fullness of grace through Christ, be steadfast in prayer. Let us not leave our homes barren of prayer, but make them little churches filled with incense rising to heaven.

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.

Can We Deliver #Prayer to Our #Home?

(part 6)

Beloved brethren, peace be to you in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Many ask: Can prayer be delivered to our home? Must the prayer of the faithful only be lifted in the temple, or does it also ascend when uttered in the quiet of the household?

The answer is found in the Scriptures and in the life of the Church: prayer is not bound by walls or doors, for wherever the faithful heart is lifted to God, there heaven opens and the angels bear it before the throne of the Almighty. The saints of old and the holy apostles have shown us the hours of prayer, each hour rich with divine mystery. Let us consider them carefully, and learn how prayer sanctifies not only the temple, but also our homes.

The Ninth Hour of Prayer

At the ninth hour what we call (9 a.m) in the afternoon the angels of God receive the prayers, supplications, and incense of mankind. This is not an invention of man, but witnessed in the Scriptures:

“Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour.” (Acts 3:1)

Cornelius, the centurion, prayed at this hour with earnest heart, and the heavens answered him. (Acts 10:3, 9)

But more than this, the ninth hour is sanctified forever, for it was at this very hour that our Lord Jesus Christ bowed His head upon the cross and delivered His holy soul into the hands of the Father. At this time, therefore, we remember His suffering, His death, His immeasurable poverty for our sake.

Thus, beloved, whether you are in the temple or in your home, sanctify the ninth hour with prayer. Call to mind the crucifixion of Christ. Let your heart be broken in remembrance of His sacrifice, and pray that as Cornelius received mercy, so also your prayer may be accepted by the holy angels and reconciled before God.

The Evening prayer( 12:00 pm)

The time of the evening prayer is as a Sabbath hour, for just as laborers receive their wages, so too the faithful receive reward for their works. Christ Himself likened the kingdom to laborers in the vineyard, each receiving from the Master his just due. (Matthew 20:1–16)

David declared: “Let my prayer be set forth before Thee as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice.” (Psalm 140:2) Elijah, at this very hour, offered his sacrifice, and the Holy Trinity accepted it in fire. (1 Kings 18:36) Ezra, likewise, humbled himself in prayer at this hour. (Ezra 9:5)

Most wondrous of all, at this time our Lord descended into the grave according to the flesh, and into hell according to the soul, to bring forth mankind from the shadow of death. (Matthew 27:45–61)

Therefore, when you pray in your home at this hour, remember that Christ entered the depths for your sake, to break open the prison of death and lead you into eternal life.

The Prayer of the Night (3:00pm)(Before Sleep)

When the day is done and night falls, the faithful commend themselves into the hands of God. We do not know what awaits us in our sleep, but the Shepherd of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps. He guards His flock by day and by night.

Thus, before resting, let every home lift up prayer. Recall the agony of Gethsemane, where the Lord prayed in the night and taught His disciples to watch with Him. (Matthew 26:36) Entrust your household to the Creator with faith, saying, “Peace be upon us, for He watches over us.”

The Midnight Prayer

David, the prophet, proclaimed: “At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto you because of your righteous judgments.” (Psalm 118:62) Midnight is no ordinary time; it is crowned with mysteries:

At midnight, Christ was born of the Virgin. (Luke 2:7–8)

At midnight, He was baptized in the Jordan. (Luke 3:21)

At midnight, He rose from the grave in triumph. (John 20:1)

At midnight, He shall come again to judge the living and the dead. (Matthew 25:6; Mark 13:35)

It was also at midnight that Paul and Silas, imprisoned in chains, lifted up songs of praise. (Acts 16:25)

Therefore, when you rise at midnight in your home to pray, recall the mysteries of Christ: His coming down from heaven, His birth of the Virgin Mary, His victory over death, and His second coming in glory. Let your prayer be filled with remembrance and thanksgiving, and ask that you may be counted worthy to stand at His right hand on the Day of Judgment.

The Diligence of the Saints

These holy hours of prayer are not merely symbols but practices sanctified by the saints. In monasteries, men and women of God endure hardship, silence, even the terrors of the night, so that they might lift prayers without ceasing. They follow the seven hours of prayer, as taught by Abba Giorgis, the Ethiopian Kyrillos, who ordered them with great devotion. Especially during Lent and the season of the Passion, the Church chants these prayers in melodies that pierce the heart and draw the soul heavenward.

What Does #Negere #Maryam Mean?

Beloved children of the Holy Church, peace and grace to you in Christ our Lord. Today we reflect on the meaning of Negere Maryam, which translates as “The Story of Mary”. This story is not simply a biography; it is a divine lesson revealing the secrets God has shared with humanity through the Most Holy Virgin Mary, the Mother of our Savior.

The Meaning of the Phrase

Negere – means “story” or “teaching.”

Maryam (Mary) – the name of the Holy Virgin.

Thus, Negere Maryam is a sacred lesson teaching us about Mary’s role in God’s plan for salvation.As the rivers of wisdom cannot be fully contained in words, so too is it impossible to exhaust the glory and mystery of Mary in a single narrative.

“In this lesson, however, let us focus on three key points.”

Three Main Points of the Story

For clarity, we focus on three principal aspects:

1. The Genealogy of the Holy Virgin Mary

2. The Meaning of the Name “Mary”

3. Additional Names by Which She Is Known

1. The Genealogy of the Holy Virgin Mary

God is holy, and wherever He dwells, that person, place, or object becomes sanctified. Our Lady Mary is called holy because she was prepared as the dwelling place of the Almighty. From her body, Christ took flesh; from her blood, He took life; from her soul, He took the purity fitting for the Incarnation. She is a saint made holy by divine choice, not by human merit, and in her, heaven and earth meet.

2. The Meaning of the Name “Mary”

The name Mary is derived from the Hebrew word (Mar-yam), meaning “mother of many.” Just as Abraham is called the father of many nations (Gen. 17:5), Mary is rightly the mother of all believers in Christ.

Church scholars further illuminate her name as signifying several profound realities:

a) The Way to the Kingdom of Heaven

Mary is the pathway through which salvation entered the world. By giving birth to Christ, she made eternal life accessible to all Adam’s descendants. All who seek the Kingdom of Heaven rely upon her intercession, for it is through her womb that the Savior of mankind came forth.

b) Grace and Wealth

Though her parents endured reproach for their faith, Mary’s birth became a wellspring of divine grace and wealth for humanity. Through her Adam, who was separated from God’s grace because of sin and crushed under the feet of demons, received grace again and became a partaker of the riches of the Holy Spirit through Our Lady.As Abba Hiriakos extols in the Liturgy : “When Adam was expelled from Paradise, you became his hope.”

c) Perfect in Body and Soul

God, who is perfect in all things, chose Mary to bear His Son. Therefore, she was made perfect in body and soul, prepared to be a pure and holy vessel for the Incarnation.

d) Above Creatures, Below the Creator

Mary is exalted above all angels and saints, not by mere grace alone, but because the Creator Himself took flesh from her. This is why Gabriel proclaimed: “Blessed are you among women” (Luke 1:28). She is above all creation under God, yet remains His servant.

e) Mother of Many

Just as a household has a head and a caretaker, all Christians who are members of Christ’s family find their spiritual mother in Mary, with Christ as the head of their household.

f) Mediator Between God and Man

Mary serves as the bridge between humanity and her Son, God incarnate. She presents human supplications to Him and brings His mercy to mankind. Through her, believers receive the blessing of body and soul, salvation and grace.

3. Additional Names of the Virgin Mary

The Church venerates her under many glorious titles, reflecting her role in the divine plan of salvation:

Mother of God (Theotokos) – she bore the Word made flesh.

Ever-Virgin – holy before, during, and after the birth of Christ.

Kidane Mihret (Covenant of Mercy) – the faithful intercessor and refuge of sinners.

Redeemer of the World – for through her came the Savior of humanity.

Conclusion

Beloved, the story of Mary—Negere Maryam—is not merely a tale of a holy woman but a revelation of divine wisdom and mercy. Through her, Christ entered the world, the grace of God was restored to mankind, and the path to salvation was opened. Let us honor her, seek her intercession, and follow her obedience and humility, that we too may be made worthy of eternal life through her Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

What #Should We #Pray?

(part 7)

Beloved brethren in Christ, children of the Holy Church, peace and grace be with you. Today we turn our hearts to a most important matter: What should we pray? For prayer is the breath of the soul, the ladder to heaven, and the key by which the faithful unlock the treasures of God’s mercy.

The Fathers of the Church, guided by the Holy Spirit, have preserved for us the prayers that sanctify each day, prayers that nourish both monks in their solitude and the faithful in their homes. Let us, then, consider these treasures of prayer one by one.

1. The Psalms of David

The Psalms are the school of prayer. From the monasteries of the desert to the homes of the faithful, the Psalms are repeated daily. The Fathers ordered that the Psalms be divided according to the days of the week, so that all 150 must be prayed regularly:

The Psalms of David, like all prayers, contain a prayer appointed for each day.Let us now take a closer look at them:

Monday → Psalms 1–30

Tuesday → Psalms 31–60

Wednesday → Psalms 61–80

Thursday → Psalms 81–110

Friday → Psalms 111–130

Saturday → Psalms 131–150

Sunday → The Prayer of the Prophets and the Song of Solomon

If one cannot recite all, the Fathers permitted the recitation of “One King”—that is, ten psalms per day.

For example, Psalms 1–10 on Monday, Psalms 31–40 on Tuesday, and so forth.Those who are unable to recite everything instead choose certain hymns and offer them each day.

2,Praises of Mary (Wudase Maryam)

No day should pass without the praise of the Holy Virgin. If possible, the Praises of Mary should be recited all the seven days praises ; if not, it is fitting to recite them daily. After completing the regular daily prayers, it is proper to recite the praises of mary for the day and thus partake in the blessings of Our Lady.”

The monks of Waldeba, the teachers and students of the Church, and all faithful souls lift up the “praises of  Mary” daily. The Virgin is the Covenant of Mercy, and through her intercession we are strengthened. Let us, therefore, make it our habit to greet her in prayer, whether at night before sleep or in the morning when we rise.

3. The Gospel of John

The daily reading of the Holy Gospel, especially the Gospel of John, Dividing it into chapters and reading it every day is counted as prayer itself. For in these words we hear the voice of Christ.The Fathers pray this prayer diligently each day.

4. Other Prayers

There are also other prayers such as the Praise of God, the remembrance of Golgotha, the appearances of Christ and His Mother, the prayers of the Book of Prayer, the Psalms, and the miracles of God. Each one prays according to their ability. But at the very least, every Christian should pray the Psalms and the Praises of Mary.

5. Short Prayers

When time is short and we cannot read long prayers, the Fathers taught us to pray short and powerful prayers such as:

Abune Zebesemayat
(The Our Father who art in heaven) 

The Prayer of Faith(tselote haymanot)

Psalm 150 (the great hymn of David)

The Hymn of Mary

Even if the prayer is brief, it seals the day with God’s blessing.

The Fathers also taught that when we pray Psalm 150, it is as though we have prayed the entire Psalter, and we receive the blessing of David. At the very least, we should never leave our homes without saying the Our Father, just as the Lord Jesus Christ commanded.

In monasteries short prayers are often used ande Short prayer may vary from place to place : nine times ( selam leki ) and twelve times (Abune zebesemayat)

6. The Order of Short Prayers

A common order of short prayers is as follows:

1. The Our Father (Abune Zebesemayat)

2. One Psalm of David

3. The Praises of Mary (Wudase Maryam) and other hymns

4. Again the (Abune Zebesemayat), followed by BeEnte Egzi’etne Maryam, the Creed (Tselote Haymanot), and the Abune Zebesemayat with Kyrie Eleison (Lord have mercy) said forty-one times.

But the Fathers also warn: if we use only short prayers every day and neglect the longer prayers, our soul may become weak and fall into temptation.

Conclusion

Prayer is not measured by length alone but by constancy and devotion. The Psalms lift our souls to heaven; the Hail Mary( selam leki) unites us to the Virgin’s intercession;the Gospel fills us with Christ’s voice; and the short prayers keep our hearts awake to God in every place and time.

Let us, therefore, not allow a single day to pass without lifting our voices in prayer. For he who prays stands in the company of angels, partakes of the blessings of the saints, and draws down upon himself the mercy of the Holy Trinity.

Beloved children of the holy Orthodox faith, I greet you with the peace of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Today we consider an essential matter for the life of the soul: What should we pray? This question is not small, for prayer is the very breath of the Christian. As the body dies when it ceases to breathe, so the soul grows faint and falls when it ceases to pray. Therefore, let us open the Scriptures, the wisdom of the Fathers, and the tradition of our Church, and learn with zeal what our Lord requires of us in prayer.

1. Short Prayers – When They Are Right, and When They Are Wrong

Sometimes, short prayers are necessary:

When we are in deep trouble, like Peter crying, “Lord, save me!”

When time does not allow us to pray long.

These are good and acceptable. New Christians may also begin with short prayers, like infants who first drink milk. but As we mature in faith, we must also grow stronger in prayer.

If we always give God only a few hurried words, and then excuse ourselves saying, “He is merciful, He will understand”, we are misusing His kindness. That is not true devotion but laziness.

The Church gives us prayers to strengthen us:

The Psalms of David,

The Hail Mary,

The liturgical prayers in the services.

These are not only for monks or priests but for all: youth, deacons, clergy, evangelists, singers, and every believer. Whoever neglects them becomes weak and easily falls into temptation.

2. The Foundation of Prayer – “Our Father”

The center of all prayer is the one Christ Himself taught us: “Our Father who art in heaven” (Abune Zebe-Semayat).

Whenever we pray, we should begin with this. If we are interrupted in the middle of prayer, we should seal that pause with “Our Father,” handle the matter, and then return to prayer, again beginning with “Our Father.”

This way, our prayers are never left unfinished or empty, but always held together by the words of Christ.

3. The Power of Prayer in the Church

Do not limit prayer to your home. The Church is the house of God, and prayers offered there are greater and more powerful than any other.

God Himself said:

“My eyes will be open and My ears attentive to the prayer made in this place. I have chosen this house; My eyes and My heart will always be there.” (2 Chronicles 7:15–16)

When the faithful gather together, led by priests, their prayer has great strength because it is united. Therefore, we should be present in church, lifting up our voices with the assembly.

4. The Sabbath and the Liturgy 

Our greatest duty is to honor the holy Sabbath and to celebrate the Liturgy .

The ancient Fathers Abba Michael and Abba Gabriel warned against those who would celebrate the Liturgy carelessly or without reverence.

We must not only come for the Eucharist itself, but also take part in the hours of prayer, psalms, and hymns before it. These are the spiritual banquet of the Church. To neglect them is to treat ourselves as strangers in our own Mother’s house.

Those who join in these prayers grow in love for the faith of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. Those who neglect them risk becoming outsiders to their own inheritance.

5. How We Should Live in Prayer

Keep the appointed times of prayer faithfully.

Pray with the words of the psalms, hymns, and intercessions.

Be present in the temple, not just alone at home.

Unite your heart to the prayers of the Liturgy daily, speaking with God as His child.

Conclusion

To pray little or not at all is to weaken the soul and expose ourselves to temptation. To pray faithfully at home, in church, and especially in the liturgy is to dwell in the protection of God.

Therefore, let us never grow lazy in prayer. Let us speak daily with our Maker, lifting our voices with His Church, He who prays dwells with God; he who abandons prayer strays into the hands of the evil one.

What #Should We #Pray? – The Prayer of Our Father

(Part 9)

Beloved brothers and sisters, Jesus   Christ Himself taught us how to pray. The Our Father is short in words, but full of meaning. Every part shows us how to live as God’s children. Let us walk through it clearly.

1. “Our Father in Heaven”

When you say “Our Father,” you are calling the Creator of all things our Father. That is a great honor. But if you continue to live in sin, how can you truly call Him our Father? To speak these words, your life must reflect them.

We add, “in heaven,” not because God is locked in heaven, but to show that He is above everything and unlike earthly fathers. Earthly fathers give us life in the flesh; the heavenly Father gives us eternal life in the spirit.

The Scripture says: “To all who received Him, He gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12). So when you pray, live as a true son or daughter of heaven.

2. “May Your Name Be Holy”

God’s name is already holy. Nothing we do can make it more holy. But people dishonor His name through sin, while others honor it through obedience.

When you pray, “May Your name be holy,” you are asking that your life and your actions shine so that people see your good works and give glory to your Father in heaven (Matthew 5:16).

3. “May Your Kingdom Come. May Your Will Be Done on Earth as in Heaven”

God’s kingdom is present wherever His will is obeyed. In heaven the angels do His will completely—quickly and joyfully.

When you pray this, you are asking that God’s will be done in your life and in the world, just as it is in heaven. It means surrendering your desires to Him, fighting against sin, and living as a true citizen of His kingdom.

4. “Give Us Today Our Daily Bread”

This prayer is not about wealth or luxury. It is about what we need to live each day. God provides food, clothing, shelter, and strength. Jesus already told us: “Seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well” (Matthew 6:33).

5. “Forgive Us Our Sins, as We Forgive Those Who Sin Against Us”

God connects His forgiveness to our forgiveness. If you forgive others, God will forgive you. If you refuse, He will not forgive you (Matthew 6:14–15).

The sinful woman was forgiven because she loved much (Luke 7:47). But the unforgiving servant was punished because he showed no mercy (Matthew 18:23–35).

So when you pray these words, search your heart. If you hold anger or hatred, your prayer condemns you instead of saving you.

6. “Do Not Let Us Fall into Temptation, but Rescue Us from Evil”

We ask God not to leave us in trials we cannot endure. Temptations will come, but without His help we are too weak. The flesh is weak, but God makes the spirit strong.

When you pray, “Rescue us from evil,” you are asking for protection from the devil, from sin, and from everything that destroys the soul.

Conclusion

The "Our Father" teaches us everything we need in prayer:

To honor God as Father,

To live so His name is glorified,

To seek His kingdom and His will,

To trust Him for daily needs,

To forgive as He forgives us,

To ask His help against temptation and evil.

Do not just repeat these words with your lips. Let them live in your heart and actions. Then you will not only pray like Christ taught you will live as a true child of the Father.

The Holy Repose of #Abune #Tekle #Haymanot, the New Apostle of Ethiopia

(Nehase 24)

Beloved in Christ, today we commemorate the repose of the great Abune Tekle Haymanot of Debre Libanos, the lamp of Ethiopia and the one called Ḥadīs Ḥawārya“the New Apostle.” His memory shines upon us on Nehase 24, together with the repose of other holy fathers and one blessed mother. Their lives, sweeter than honey, are preserved for us as a treasury of faith and endurance.

The Birth and Divine Election of the Saint

Abune Tekle Haymanot his name meaning “ Plant of the faith ” was conceived by the divine will through the helping of the Archangel Michael, to his father, the priest Tsega Zeab, and to his holy mother egzi harya. His birth took place on Tahisas 24, 1197 A.D., yet even before his coming into the world, he was set apart as a chosen vessel.

On the third day of his infancy, he descended from his mother’s arms and proclaimed: “Holy is the Father, Holy is the Son, Holy is the Holy Spirit.” Thus, from his very lips, God’s praise was perfected, as from the mouth of a nursing babe (Psalm 8:2).

The Heavenly Calling

Trained by his father in the sacred liturgy, he was ordained by the Archbishop of Alexandria, Abune Kerlos, and thus consecrated to the service of the Church from his youth. But his destiny was confirmed in the wilderness, where the Archangel Michael appeared and commanded him to abandon the hunting of beasts, and instead to hunt souls for salvation.

Michael announced to him the gifts bestowed by Christ: power to raise the dead, heal the sick, cast out demons, and turn hearts from idols to the true worship of God. The Lord Himself also appeared, blessing him and granting him the apostolic authority first given to the disciples: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven; whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.”

“Your name shall no longer be Fisḥa tsyōn (Joy of Zion), but Tekle Haymanot. Its meaning is : the Plant of Father, the Plant of Son, and the Plant of Holy Spirit." and From that day, Tekle Haymanot became the new apostle of Ethiopia. with Michael as his unfailing guardian.

His Ministry Across Ethiopia

From that hour, Tekle Haymanot devoted his life to the Gospel. He renounced his possessions, giving them to the poor and to the Church, declaring: “O Lord Jesus Christ! I have left open my house on earth, so that You may open the gate of heaven for me.”

Then he began to travel and preach:

Turning people from sin to righteousness.

Turning people from idolatry to the worship of the true God.

Preached in Damot and Wolayta for 12 years, destroying idol worship and planting the faith.and building churches upon the ruins of false worship. Lived in monasteries across Ethiopia, including Debre Damo, Debre Libanos, and Asbo.
In Tigray and Debre Damo, he embraced the monastic life, enduring hardship and performing countless miracles.

Through his labors, monasteries multiplied, disciples were gathered, and entire peoples were illumined with the light of Christ. Truly, Ethiopia received him as her apostle, and his ministry was adorned with wonders beyond number.

The Trials and Ascetic Struggle

The saint’s ascetic feats are awe-inspiring. By divine strength, he was given six radiant wings when the devil sought to destroy him, and he flew as a cherub. He shattered idols, healed the sick, and humbled dragons through the sign of the cross.

Yet his greatest struggle was not against beasts or demons, but against his own flesh. For seven years he stood upon one leg, like a pillar unshaken, fasting without food or water.It was only in the fourth year of the seven years that they tasted a little water. His cane broke beneath him from long vigils, yet he persevered, until the Lord appeared, clothing him with fire and crowning him with seven crowns of life:

For his pure faith,

For his journeys across Ethiopia,

For his sufferings against idolatry,

For his pilgrimages to Jerusalem,

For his fasting and ceaseless prayer,

For his monastic labors,

For his blood shed in the struggle for the faith.

Thus, even before his death, Christ granted him a vision of his heavenly inheritance.

His Final Admonitions

As his repose drew near, he spoke to his disciples with fatherly counsel:

“Not every monk enters the kingdom of heaven, but only those who despise the world. Seek first the righteousness of God. Fast and pray. Love one another. Do not love the fleeting glory of the world, but imitate the fathers of old, who conquered evil through toil and tears. If you share not their sufferings, you will not share their joy.”

He urged them to be free from worldly vanities, to serve the Church without ceasing, and to remain steadfast in prayer and charity. Then, blessing them, he commended his soul to God.

His Glorious Repose and Promise

On Nehase 24, 1296 Abune Tekle Haymanot entered into rest. Christ appeared with His Virgin Mother and the holy angels, receiving his pure soul with honor. The angels cried: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His saints” (Psalm 116:15).

He was buried at Debre Asbo, which later became Debre Libanos, and after 57 years his relics were transferred with great solemnity. The Lord promised that no soul invoking the name of Tekle Haymanot whether righteous or sinner would be left without his intercession before the throne of God.

His Feasts

The Church celebrates his holy life in several feasts:

His conception, Megabit 24, 1196

His birth, Tahsas 24, 1197

His ordination, Hidar 24, 1197

The breaking of his leg through prayer, Tir 4, 1289

His repose, Nehase 24, 1296

The Holy Life of #Kristos #Semra (Feast: #Nehase 24)

Beloved in Christ, today we turn our hearts to the luminous memory of Holy Mother Kristos Semra, the fragrant flower of Shewa, the glory of Zion, and the chosen staff of the Holy Virgin Mary. Her story is not merely history; it is a divine testimony, a mirror of faith, a torch of endurance, and a ladder leading heavenward.

Her Birth and Early Life

Holy Kristos Semra was born in Geye, Shewa Bulga Province, from faithful parents her father Deresani and her mother Eleni. Like the righteous of old, they nurtured their daughter in the fear of God, raising her in the holy order of the Church, and instructing her in the books of both the Old and New Testaments.

When she came of age, they gave her in marriage to Semre Giorgis, son of Eyesus Moa. The Lord blessed their union with twelve children ten sons and two daughters. Yet, unlike many who are distracted by worldly care, Kristos Semra raised her children in discipline and in the law of God, sowing in them the seed of eternal life.

The King’s Praise and the Vision of St. Michael

In those days reigned the merciful Emperor Gebre Meskel. Hearing of her beauty, her kindness, and her renown, he counted her among the 174 most admirable women of his kingdom. In his favor, he sent 272 young servants to attend to her.

But Kristos Semra, fearing the vanity of earthly praise, turned her heart to God in prayer. And lo! the Archangel Michael appeared to her in vision, greeting her with the heavenly salutation:

“Peace be with you, beloved Kristos Semra. Eat of the bread of heaven, which is the goodness of God.and he fed her”

Filled with the Holy Spirit, she gave thanks to her Creator. With the servants sent by the king, she built a church in honor of St. Michael, just as the Archangel had commanded her.

Her Ministry and the Miracle of Resurrection

She brought the Ark of the Angel into that holy temple and served God with devotion. Yet trials were not far from her path. One day, a servant girl fell under the power of an unclean spirit and resisted her mistress’s counsel. Soon after, the girl died, and Kristos Semra wept bitterly, lamenting:

“This death shall be accounted as my own sin, O Lord!”

In her grief, she prayed to God, and He, the Creator of life, raised the girl from the dead. Overcome with joy, she declared:

“If the Lord works such wonders for me while still in this passing world, how much more glorious will His gifts be in the life to come!”

Her Renunciation and Life of Asceticism

Strengthened in spirit, she left her husband, her children, and her household, taking with her only her youngest son. She entered the holy monastery of Debre Libanos, where she dedicated herself to fasting and prayer.

Yet even here, her life was marked by sorrow mingled with glory. When her child was taken into Paradise by the Archangel Michael, she was pierced with grief. But the Archangel comforted her with the revelation that her son rejoices eternally in the kingdom of God.

Led thereafter to Lake Tana, she spent twelve years immersed in the waters, standing in prayer until her body became swollen and even the fish passed through her. Yet Christ appeared to her, granting her ten crowns from heaven and surrounding her with the guardianship of the Archangels Michael, Gabriel, Raphael and above all, His holy Mother, the Virgin Mary.

Her Compassion and Intercession

Burning with divine charity, Kristos Semra prayed even for the enemy of mankind:

“O my Creator, have mercy on the devil, for You have preserved me from his snares. I ask this for the sake of Adam and his children, that he may not deceive them, for their flesh is my flesh.”

The Lord, marveling at her supplication, commanded St. Michael to take her even to Hell. There she spoke with Satan himself, who mocked her attempt at reconciliation and cast her into the flames. But Michael struck Hell with his sword, opening a path of deliverance. And behold! 10,000 souls clung to the radiance of her spirit and were brought forth with her into freedom.

Her Glory and Her Rest

The Lord Jesus Christ promised her a place of rest at the right hand of the Holy Virgin Mary, and He gave her the name:

“The Staff of Mary.”

The Holy Virgin appeared to her and blessed her with words of praise:

“Blessed is the womb that bore you, and blessed the breasts that nursed you. Blessed are the eyes that beheld you, and blessed are those who celebrate your struggle.”

At last, she prepared for her departure. Digging a pit equal to her height, she set spears around her and endured twelve years in this manner of worship, pierced and suffering, yet unwavering. Then, on Nehase 24, her soul was received by the angels, and her body was laid to rest in Geye Monastery, where her holy relics remain for the blessing of the faithful.

The Lord’s Promise

The Lord Himself declared to her:

“I will bless twelve generations of those who love you, who call upon your name, who honor your memory, and who celebrate your feast.”

Thus, her name is glorified, her prayers intercede for us, and her memory remains a fountain of blessing until the end of the age.

Conclusion

O beloved faithful, let us imitate the steadfastness of Holy Kristos Semra—her courage in trial, her compassion even for her enemies, her ceaseless prayer, and her trust in the Lord who crowned her.

May her prayers, her intercession, and her unfailing aid be with us all, now and forever.

#Prostration – What Does It Mean?

(Part 1)

Dear friends who follow the Orthodox teachings transmitted by the website of John the Repentant, we greet you with the greetings of God. Today, based on the above-mentioned topic, we have sent you the following important lesson and we entrust you to read and learn from it:

What is Prostration?

Prostration means to bow, kneel, fall on your face, touch the forehead to the ground, and rise again. It is an outward act through which we express our submission to the Creator, and our reverence for those who are exalted in glory, grace, holiness, and life.

Prostration and Humility

“Humbleness” is shown when we acknowledge that we are God’s creation, and that we cannot accomplish anything without His help. As the Lord said: “Without Me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Thus we confess: “Almighty God, You alone are everything. We are nothing without You. To You belong adoration, honor, praise, sacrifice, and worship.” In prostration, we lower ourselves before His feet and reveal our submission.

Two Kinds of Prostration

There are two kinds of prostration:

1. Prostration of Worship – offered only to God, the Creator.

2. Prostration of Grace – offered in reverence to the Holy Virgin Mary, the holy angels, the righteous, and the martyrs.

Prostration of Worship

When we prostrate before God, it is the prostration of worship. As it is written: “Worship the Lord your God, and serve Him only” (Luke 4:8). We bow to our Creator who made us in His image and likeness.

The Holy Church teaches us to say: “I bow to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”

With reverence, we imitate the heavenly angels who bow before Him.

Prostration is done in the holy place, within the Church, before the holy icons.

But this act must be joined with purity of heart: when we bow, we must do so with a conscience free from evil, with fear of God, and with sincerity, touching our forehead to the ground.

Words of Prostration

The faithful say:

“I bow to the Father, I bow to the Son, I bow to the Holy Spirit. Glory to the Father, glory to the Son, glory to the Holy Spirit. Glory to You for blessing us, for bringing us to this hour, for keeping us in Your goodness, and guiding us with Your light.”

“Hallelujah to the Father, Hallelujah to the Son, Hallelujah to the Holy Spirit. Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal.”

Prostration in the Life of the Church

Fasting, prayer, almsgiving, and prostration are the spiritual weapons by which we discipline the body and submit ourselves to God. Prostration is not only for mankind but also for the angels:

“…let all His angels worship Him” (Psalm 96:7).

“Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory” (Isaiah 6:3).

Thus, prostration is part of the eternal worship before the throne of God. And for us, it is also the path to fulfill our very purpose: man was created to worship God and to inherit His glory.

Conclusion

Prostration is more than a bodily action. It is the sign of humility, the confession of our nothingness, and the exaltation of God’s majesty. It unites us with the heavenly host who ceaselessly bow before Him, and it fulfills the reason for our creation: to glorify God and partake in His eternal life.

The #Purpose of #Prostration

(Part 2)

Beloved in Christ, children of the holy Orthodox Church, grace and peace be unto you. Today let us meditate upon the sacred mystery of prostration, that ancient gesture of worship which the Holy Scriptures commend, and which the Fathers of the Church have faithfully preserved. For the body bows in humility, yet the soul soars in exaltation; the knees bend low, yet the heart rises to heaven. What, then, is the purpose of prostration?

1. Prostration of Worship — to God Alone

The first type is the prostration of worship. This is given only to God, because only He is divine by nature.

When we bow to God, we bow to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

This is why our prayer says: “I prostrate for the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, one prostrate .”

The word “one worship,” we do not count the number of prostrations, but rather affirm that the act is directed to the one God ( for The Father, The Son, The Holy Sprite ), and to no other. Neither angel nor man, nor any created thing, may receive such adoration. To offer it elsewhere would be idolatry, a theft of the glory due to God.

This kind of prostration must never be given to any creature not to people, angels, or things made by human hands. God warned His people:

“You shall not worship any other gods before me” (Exodus 20:3).

“For I, the Lord your God, am a jealous God” (Exodus 20:5).

To give worship to anyone else is to provoke God’s anger. Worship belongs to Him alone, for He is our Creator, Redeemer, and the source of all life.

2. Prostration of Grace

The second type is the prostration of honor,or the prostration of grace. This is not prostration of God’s divine nature, but honor shown to the saints, to the Virgin Mary, and even to the Holy Cross.

After we confess “I worship the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit,” our prayers continue with words of honor:

“I bow to our Lady, the Virgin Mary, who gave birth to God, and to the Cross on which Christ was crucified for the life of the world.”

This shows the difference:

Worship is only for God.

Honor is given to those whom God has sanctified and filled with His grace.

When we bow before Mary, we do not worship her as God. We honor her because she bore God in the flesh.When we bow before the Cross, we do not worship the wood, but honor it because it carried Christ and became the instrument of our salvation.

The Bible itself supports this kind of honor. Isaac blessed Jacob with these words:

“Let nations serve you, and princes bow down to you; be lord over your brothers, and let your father’s sons bow down to you. Cursed be he who curses you, and blessed be he who blesses you” (Genesis 27:29).

Though Esau was the firstborn, God gave Jacob the blessing. From that moment, God was called the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The act of bowing before Jacob was not worship of him as God, but honor for the grace God placed upon him.

3,What Prostration Teaches Us

Prostration has a deep spiritual meaning.

Bowing down shows humility, that we are dust before God.

Touching the ground reminds us of our weakness and mortality.

Rising again points to our hope of resurrection in Christ.

Thus, every prostration becomes a silent sermon. It teaches us humility, reminds us of God’s holiness, and strengthens our faith in eternal life.

Conclusion

So then, we must keep these two truths in our hearts:

1. Prostration of Worship — belongs to God alone: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

2. Prostration of Grace — belongs to the saints, to the Virgin Mary, and to the Cross, because God’s grace shines through them.

When we worship God, we confess His majesty.When we honor His saints, we glorify the God who sanctified them.

What Is the #Purpose of #Prostration?

(Part 3)

Beloved brothers and sisters, today we continue our meditation on the holy mystery of prostration. This act of bowing down is not a human invention, but a sacred gesture found throughout the Scriptures. Both in the Old and New Testaments, we see prophets, kings, and apostles bowing before God and His chosen servants. The Church, guided by the Holy Spirit, has preserved this tradition and ordered it with wisdom.

1. The Witness of the Old Testament

When Moses longed to know the name of his God, the Lord revealed Himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — the God who blessed Jacob through Isaac and gave him the inheritance. In this revelation, we see blessing and covenant.

Obadiah, the commander of King Ahab’s army, bowed before Elijah, saying, “My lord” (1 Kings 18:8).

The captain of fifty, sent by King Ahaziah with his soldiers, bowed down before Elijah and pleaded, “O man of God, let my life and the lives of these fifty servants of yours be precious in your sight” (2 Kings 1:13). Because he bowed and honored the prophet, his prayer was heard, and he and his men were spared from the fire of heaven.

The men of Jericho bowed before Elisha when they saw that the spirit of Elijah rested upon him (2 Kings 2:15).

The Shunammite woman bowed before Elisha in her sorrow when her child died, and again in her joy when the child was restored to life (2 Kings 4:27–37).

2. The Witness of the New Testament

The New Testament also shows us the same reverence:

The jailer at Philippi, trembling with fear, bowed down before Paul and Silas after the earthquake shook the prison and their chains fell away (Acts 16:29).

These examples show that bowing is not only fitting but also powerful, for God accepts humility and honors reverence.

3.The Three Orders of Prostration

The Holy Church teaches us that prostration is not all of one kind. There are three orders of prostration:

(a) Full Prostration — Wediq

This is to fall completely to the ground, with forehead, fingers, and knees touching the earth.

“He bowed his face to the ground” (Gen. 19:1).

“He bowed down and worshiped” (Num. 22:31; John 5:15).

“He fell at his feet and worshiped him” (Acts 10:25).

“I fell at his feet to worship him” (Rev. 19:10).

This is the most complete form of surrender and humility before God.

B) Kneeling Prostration(astebrko)

This is done by bending the knees and lowering the body. It is what St. Paul meant when he wrote: “…that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow” (Phil. 2:10).

The hymn of the Church proclaims: “Standing on our knees, by the will of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, we bow down and worship Christ who raised us up to salvation.”

(c) Bowing of the Head — (Adnon)

This is a gentler form of reverence, where the head, forehead, and neck are inclined. At the close of the Divine Liturgy the deacon prays: “Save “‘Humble yourselves before the Lord our God…’ — this is what He is saying.”


4. Times When We Do Not Bow

The Church, in her wisdom, has also set aside holy times when bowing is not practiced. These include:

On Sundays, the day of the Resurrection.

On Saturdays, the first day of the week.

On the feast of Pentecost and during its season.

On the feasts of the Lord.

On the feast of the Virgin Mary.

On the feast of Saint Michael.

After we accept Eucharist 

But if these feasts fall on the Day of the Passion or on the Feast of the Cross, then prostration is performed, for those days recall the Lord’s suffering and His victory through the Cross.

5. Words of Worship

The prayers of the Church guide our bows and prostrations. When we prostrate always we need to say:-

I prostrate before the Father.

I prostrate before the Son.

I prostrate before the Holy Spirit.

And we proclaim:

Glory be to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Hallelujah to the Father, Hallelujah to the Son, Hallelujah to the Holy Spirit.

Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Living, Holy El Shaddai, Holy Adonai, Holy Yahweh, Holy Hosts, Holy Jesus, Holy Christ, Holy Emmanuel glory to the Son of the Virgin Mary.

6. The Penitential Adoration

In times of repentance we cry out with bowed bodies and contrite hearts:

Kyrie Eleison, Jesus.

Kyrie Eleison, Christ.

Kyrie Eleison, Emmanuel.

Lord Christ, have mercy.

Lord God, have mercy.

Lord Savior, have mercy.

Lord Son of the Virgin Mary, have mercy.

These words, joined with prostration, are the visible tears of the soul, pleading for mercy from our Savior.

Conclusion

Beloved, prostration is not an empty motion of the body, but a holy act of faith. In it we confess our weakness, honor God’s majesty, revere His saints, and repent of our sins. It is rooted in Scripture, practiced by the prophets, embraced by the apostles, and ordered by the Church.

Let us therefore bow with understanding: fully to God in worship, to His saints in reverence, and in repentance for our sins. For in every bow, we humble ourselves; in every kneeling, we confess Christ’s lordship; in every rising, we proclaim our hope in His resurrection.
