The Mystery of the #Cloud: Its Creation and Its Meaning

(Part 1)

Beloved in Christ, peace and blessing to you from the Lord who governs heaven and earth, who establishes the boundaries of the seas, who gathers the waters, and who clothes the skies with clouds. Today let us reflect on the divine mystery of the cloud what it is, how it was created, and what hidden message it contains for us who believe.

The Ordering of the Waters

In the beginning, when God made the heavens and the earth, He arranged the waters in wondrous fashion. The Scriptures bear witness that He separated them and appointed their places.

One part He raised up, calling it the expanse, the firmament stretched out between earth and heaven.

Another portion of the waters, which He placed above the expanse, He called the sea.

The last portion He divided into seven parts, and the last seventh part, he called ocean, the great deep which surrounds the earth.

The solid part beneath He called the earth, which He adorned with fruitfulness and gave as a dwelling place for mankind.

Behold how our God, with wisdom, arranged even the waters in order and harmony, so that the creation might reflect His majesty.

The Birth of the Cloud

After this ordering, the Lord brought forth yet another wonder: He caused dry vapor to rise from the dry land and moist vapor to rise from the sea. From their mingling, He formed the cloud, that light and smoke-like creation which floats above the green earth.

The Psalmist declares: “He causes the vapors to ascend from the ends of the earth” (Psalm 134:7). Thus, the cloud is not of heavy substance, but of delicate and unseen particles, gathered together by the word of the Lord.

The Nature and Work of the Cloud

What is a cloud? It is a subtle, smoke-like body, invisible to touch, yet powerful in purpose. It is the chosen vessel that bears rain.

Through the mystery of evaporation, the waters of the seas and rivers are lifted upward. They are gathered into the cloud, and when the Lord commands, they are poured forth again upon the earth. But notice, brethren, how wisely God has ordered it: the waters do not descend in confusion or destruction, but in measure and in season, “filtered,” as it were, through the very body of the cloud, so that they fall gently and fruitfully.

This is why Saint Epiphanius, in his holy liturgy, testifies: “He causes the rain to fall in the wilderness where there is no man.” Mark the wonder! Even where no man dwells, where no eye beholds, the Lord waters the desert. Why? To show that His goodness is not limited to human need, but extends over all creation.

He sends the snow upon the desolate places, and pours water where men dwell. Each has its appointed place: the wilderness clothed in snow, the city refreshed with rain. Behind this, the Fathers discern a greater mystery.

The Hidden Mystery Revealed

Yet this is not all. The cloud bears within it a spiritual mystery. Just as rain is poured forth from heaven through the hidden work of God, so also did our Lord Jesus Christ come down to us.

By the unfathomable wisdom of the Father, the eternal Son was conceived without seed in the womb of the Holy Virgin Mary, overshadowed by the Holy Spirit, as a hidden cloud bearing the water of life. He came down upon the barren desert of this world, and made the wilderness of our hearts fruitful by His grace.

And when He had accomplished His saving work teaching, healing, suffering, dying, and rising again He sent forth His holy apostles, as streams of living water, to carry His Gospel to all nations. For He Himself commanded them: “Go and teach” (Matthew 28:19).

Thus, the mystery of the cloud points us to the Incarnation, the life-giving descent of Christ, and the apostolic mission which continues to water the whole earth with the teaching of truth.

Conclusion

Therefore, beloved, when you see the clouds in the heavens, lift up your hearts to the Creator. Do not regard them as mere accidents of nature, but as instruments of God’s wisdom. See in them both His providence for the body and His mystery for the soul.

The cloud teaches us of rain that refreshes the earth, and of Christ who refreshes mankind. The cloud reveals to us that our God is both Creator and Redeemer, who provides bread for the body and grace for the spirit.

When and How Much is the #Prostration #Offered for #Worship? How is it Called?

(Part 4)

Beloved brethren in Christ, peace and grace be multiplied unto you. Today we turn to a sacred question: When is prostration offered? How much is required of us? And what does the Church call this holy act? Let us attend carefully, for in these mysteries we are taught how to humble the body so that the soul may ascend to God.

1. Where Should We Pray?

God, who is infinite and uncontained, is not bound by any place. He is higher than the heavens, deeper than the abyss, and His presence stretches from horizon to horizon. Yet we, being finite creatures bound by space and time, are in need of holy places to direct our prayer.

Therefore, we gather in the temple of God the Church. Church means both the dwelling of Christ in His people, and the gathering place of the faithful. When we call the Church the dwelling of Christ, we mean His presence in the souls of the righteous, in the individual believer, and in the community. When we call the Church the house of Christ, we speak of the consecrated building where His people assemble.

Thus, the Church is the house of God Himself. It is the place where His name is called, His glory proclaimed, and the sacrifice of thanksgiving is continually offered. Wherever the faithful gather, there is the Church; for He has promised: “Where two or three are gathered in My name, there am I in their midst” (Matthew 18:20).

The first reason we worship in the Church is because it is His house, and where the King is, there His servants the holy angels and the righteous saints also dwell. We bow with reverence before God and honor those who serve Him.

2. How Do We Prostrate ?

 We bend our hips, fall upon our knees, and touch the ground with our hands and forehead. Why? Because though God is everywhere present, He Himself declares: “Heaven is My throne, and the earth is My footstool” (Matthew 5:35). When therefore we touch the earth with our heads, we humble ourselves at His feet, acknowledging His majesty.

In this way, both the worship that belongs to God alone (the prostration of His nature) and the honor shown to His saints (the prostration of grace) are performed outwardly in the same act yet the heart distinguishes their meaning.

When prostration is made in church, we turn to the East, for the Sun of Righteousness rose from the East. If we are not in a church, we set before us a holy sign: a cross, the Gospel, or an icon. Having bowed, we seal our prayer with the words: “O God, have mercy on us, and through the Virgin Mary, have mercy on us.”

In prayers of repentance, our spiritual father appoints how many prostrate and prayers we should perform, guiding us as a physician prescribes medicine. 

Whoever is moved by zeal may increase their prayers; whoever is weak may offer as they can but always remembering the sufferings of Christ. for the prostrations that we offer no strict limit is set.

3. When Should We Pray?

The angels in heaven never cease crying: “Holy, holy, holy.” The saints, despising worldly honors, forsaking earthly pleasures, dwelling in deserts and caves, spend their lives in unceasing prayer, striking their body and offering their whole being to God.

But as for us, who live amidst the cares of the world, the Church in her mercy teaches us at least this: let us pray in the morning and in the evening. If there is a church near, let us hasten to it at those hours. If not, let us imitate the prophet Daniel, who prayed in his house facing East.

Whenever we stand to pray, whether in church or at home, let us believe that we stand in spirit before the throne of the heavenly King. We begin with a bow in the name of the Holy Trinity. If even earthly kings are greeted with uplifted hands, how much more should we bow before the Eternal King?

During prayer, let us not rush. Rather, let us fall in prostration as often as the Spirit stirs us, giving thanks, marveling at His works, testifying to His glory, and offering Him our whole heart.

Even outside the appointed times of prayer, let us not pass the house of God as though it were common. For the Lord has said: “My eyes and My heart will be there forever.”

Therefore, when we pass by the Church, let us greet her, saying: “Peace be to you, O Jerusalem, heavenly city of God.” Let every opportunity become a moment of bowing, and every bowing an ascent of the soul to heaven.

5127:
The Feast of Our Fathers #Abraham, #Isaac, and #Jacob (#Nehase 28)

Beloved in Christ, today the Church gathers us into the holy mystery of remembrance. On the twenty-eighth day of Nehase, we celebrate the feast of the righteous patriarchs: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. These fathers are not merely figures of history, but pillars of faith, roots of the covenant, and living examples of obedience, humility, and trust in the Most High.

Let us, therefore, with reverence, recount their lives, not to glorify men, but to magnify the Lord who worked wonders through them. For as the Scriptures proclaim, “God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared for them a city” (Hebrews 11:16).

The Glory of the Patriarchs

The kingdom of heaven itself is adorned with their names, for Christ declared: “Many will come from the east and the west and will sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 8:11). Their righteousness shines more numerous than the stars, and their faith is counted as everlasting treasure. What tongue can fully tell their glory? What pen can describe their holiness? It is enough for us to fall in awe before their Creator and cry, “Glory! Glory! To God who is wondrous in His saints.”

Abraham: The Friend of God

Abraham, the father of faith, began his journey amidst idols, for his father Terah fashioned them. Yet, seeking the true God, Abraham saw the emptiness of wood and stone. He mocked their lifelessness, saying: “Eyes they have, but they see not; ears they have, but they hear not.” He shattered the false gods and set his heart upon the living Lord.

He departed to Canaan, trusting only in the promise of God. He faced famine, sojourned in Egypt and Palestine, yet in all these, the Creator honored him. Kings trembled before him, prophets were healed by his prayer, and strangers were welcomed into his tent. His hospitality was so great that he would not taste food unless it was shared with a guest. And behold, the Lord rewarded him: the Holy Trinity itself came to him in the plains of Mamre. and by his humility washed the feet of the Godhead.

He pleaded before the Lord for Sodom and Gomorrah, showing both mercy and boldness in intercession. And when tested, he did not withhold his beloved son but offered him upon the altar. For this obedience, he is called father of prophets, apostles, kings, and priests the very root of the covenant.

So beloved was he, that the angels proclaimed him:

“Abraham, friend of God”

“Abraham, faithful to God”

“Abraham, beloved of God”

Even in the place of the dead, God granted him a resting place of honor, shielding him from the reach of demons, until the coming of Christ.

Our father Abraham is honored in glory, holiness, and grace from Genesis to the Revelation of John. The saints invoke the Creator in his name. Because of his holiness, even the forces of darkness could not approach him. Abraham rested in peace one thousand nine hundred years before the birth of Christ, having lived one hundred and seventy-five years

Isaac: The Model of Obedience

Isaac, son of the promise, born by divine intervention, was pure and blameless. In him we behold the image of Christ, for he was the willing sacrifice. When Abraham, in obedience, bound him upon the altar, Isaac did not resist. He said instead, “Bind me, father, lest I move against you; cover my eyes, lest your heart be softened with pity.”

O wondrous obedience! O holy humility! For this reason, we honor him saying: “Peace be upon Isaac, who was faithful to his father.”

God spared his life, revealing the mystery of Christ’s coming sacrifice. Isaac lived one hundred and eighty years, walking in holiness. With his wife Rebecca, he conceived Jacob and Esau. At his passing, a heavenly voice declared:

“I will honor him who honors my friend Isaac.”

“Who bows in his name, who prays in his name, who shows mercy in his name I will reward him in heaven.”

Thus Isaac rests, adorned with blessings and eternal glory.

Jacob: The Chosen of God

Jacob, the third patriarch, followed in the footsteps of his fathers. Receiving the blessing of the firstborn, he fled to Syria. Along the way, he lay upon a stone and beheld a wondrous vision: a golden ladder reaching to heaven, with angels ascending and descending. This ladder is the mystery of the Virgin Mary, through whom the Son of God descended to earth.

Jacob proclaimed, “This is the house of God and the gate of heaven.”

He became the father of twelve sons, from whom came prophets, priests, kings, and judges—the holy nation of Israel. After serving his uncle Laban twenty-one years, he returned to Canaan, where he wrestled with God Himself. In that struggle of love, he was renamed Israel, “he who prevails with God.”

Saint Jacob suffered greatly in his old age. His sons sold their brother Joseph and deceived him, saying, ‘He has been devoured by wild beasts.’ Grieving without comfort, Jacob wept until he lost his sight. Later, when famine struck the land, he went down to Egypt with about seventy-five members of his household at the age of one hundred and thirty. There he lived for seventeen years, and at the age of one hundred and forty-seven he died, and his sons buried him with honor.

Their Eternal Feast

On Nehase 28, the Church celebrates the feast of our holy fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. They are honored as pillars of faith, and heaven itself is called by their name. Their glory is greater than the stars, and in remembering them we glorify their Creator, saying: “Glory to God who is wondrous in His saints!”

The #Days and #Times When #Prostration Is #Offered and When It Is Not Offered

(Part 5)

Dear brothers and sisters, the Holy Church has given us clear teaching about prostration. She shows us the days and times when it should be offered and the days when it should not. These rules are not given by chance, but are established with wisdom, so that we may worship God in the right way and at the right time.

Days When Prostration Is Withheld

First, let us understand when it is not permitted to prostrate. For the Church, like a wise mother, teaches that not every day is the same, nor every hour alike.

Saturdays and Sundays are exempt from prostration. For these are the days of joy, the days of rest, the days in which the light of the Resurrection shines. How can one bow in mourning on the day that Christ has triumphed over death?

Likewise, on the great feasts of the Lord His conception, His birth, His baptism, His triumphal entry on Hosanna, His resurrection, His ascension, His descent of the Spirit at Pentecost, and His glory revealed upon Mount Tabor the Church forbids prostration. These are days not of lament but of jubilation, not of abasement but of exaltation, for on these days Christ revealed His power and majesty.

In addition, on the feasts of the holy ones Our Lady on the 21st, Saint Michael on the 12th, and the Fathers on the 29th we do not bow to the ground, for the joy of the saints is shared by the faithful.

Thus, let all understand: there is a difference between the reverence we show when entering the church, bowing before the cross, venerating the holy Gospel, or greeting the holy icons, and the canonical act of prostration that belongs to the ordered life of the Church. The teaching on prostration does not refer to every gesture of adoration, but specifically to the prostration established as a permanent canon of the Church.

Days and Times When Prostration Is Commanded

Yet the Church, like a skillful physician, also prescribes for us the times when prostration is necessary, when the soul must humble itself before God in body as well as in spirit.

When we are given a special canon of penance, we must prostrate.

When we hear the words of Scripture that call us to worship, we must prostrate.

During the Divine Liturgy, when the Church proclaims, “Worship God with fear,” “Pray,” “Humble yourselves in repentance,” then let every knee bend, for heaven itself bends in awe before the mysteries.

During the time of the Passion, in the holy and great week, the Church orders us to prostrate with fasting, prayer, and tears, for then we walk with Christ in His suffering.

During the holy fasts, we must sanctify the season with prayer, almsgiving, tears, and prostration, so that our fasting may be acceptable to the Lord.

In the life of penance, when the Scriptures declare, “Humble yourselves, you who are in penance,” let us fall to the ground, for the Fathers taught their children that prostration is inseparable from repentance.

Even in our daily prayer, when we say:
“Peace be upon the Holy Church, the image of the heavenly Jerusalem, the dwelling of the Godhead, the model of Him who has set us free from sin,”
the very words call us to bend low, for the soul cannot utter such words without humbling the body before the Lord.

Thus, before the cross, before the holy Scriptures, before the images of the saints, before the Gospel of life, let every Christian prostrate in faith.

The Words of Prostration

But what shall we say as we prostrate? With the tongue we invoke the name of God; with the heart we remember the sufferings of Christ; with the soul we beg for forgiveness of our sins. Let each man say:

“O Lord, forgive us, remember not our iniquities. Have mercy on us, not according to our righteousness, but according to Your abundant kindness. You are our Creator, our King, our Shepherd, our Savior. To You alone we bow in faith and submission.”

This is the voice of true prostration: not empty motion, but the offering of the heart.

The Measure of Prostration

And how much shall we bow? The Church teaches that the number of our prostrations is not left to chance or habit but is guided by spiritual fathers. For one hundred prostrations offered in love will receive from God a hundredfold reward. Two hundred, three hundred, or more, each shall be reckoned, for God does not forget even the smallest act of service.

If the prostration is made in penance, then the measure is given by the Fathers according to the weight of sin, and the penitent bows as medicine for the soul. If it is offered freely out of love, then the Lord receives it as an offering of devotion.

Be assured, brethren, that no labor of ours is wasted before God. For He who weighs the hairs of our head and the drops of rain also weighs every prostration, every bow, every tear, and grants to His children the reward of their faithfulness.

Conclusion

Therefore, let us keep the wisdom of the Church with reverence. Let us prostrate when commanded, and in all things glorify Christ who bowed the heavens and came down for our salvation.

What does a #cloud #represent?”

(Part 2)

Beloved in Christ, peace and grace be multiplied to you. Today let us reflect on the mystery of the cloud in Holy Scripture. What does the cloud signify? What does it reveal to us about God, His saints, and His holy Mother, the Virgin Mary? The Church, following the words of the prophets, apostles, and evangelists, teaches us that the cloud is not an only mere natural wonder, but a holy sign of God’s presence, His protection, and His glory.

1. The Cloud and the Virgin Mary

St. John the Theologian writes: “And the woman fled into the wilderness, to a place prepared by God, that they should feed her there for one thousand two hundred and sixty days” (Rev. 12:6). This woman is none other than the Virgin Mary, who fled into exile, carrying her Son, the Creator of the worlds. She wandered as a refugee, holding Him who Himself appointed the bounds of creation, yet who, in His humility, allowed Himself to be borne in her arms.

When the dragon was cast down, he pursued the woman, but she was given two wings of a great eagle to fly into the wilderness (Rev. 12:13–15). The Fathers call her a swift cloud, bearing within her the Sun of Righteousness. Isaiah had spoken long before: “Heaven is My throne, and the earth is My footstool” (Isa. 66:1). She carried Him who fills all things, once in her arms, once upon her back, as she journeyed through the deserts of Egypt and into Ethiopia.

Blessed was Ethiopia, for she received the Virgin and her Child. Habakkuk foresaw this, saying: “I saw the tents of Ethiopia in affliction, and the curtains of Midian trembled” (Hab. 3:7). Thus Ethiopia rejoiced, offering love and humility in welcoming the Mother and her Son.

2. The Cloud as the Glory of God

The cloud in Scripture is a revelation of God’s majesty. In the days of Moses, God appeared in the tabernacle of meeting as a pillar of cloud. “When Moses entered the tabernacle, the pillar of cloud descended and stood at the door, and God spoke with him” (Exod. 33:8–9).

When Solomon completed the great Temple, again the cloud descended: “The house of the Lord was filled with the cloud, so that the priests could not stand to minister, for the glory of the Lord filled the house” (1 Kings 8:10).

In the New Testament, on Mount Tabor, the Lord revealed His divine light to Peter, James, and John. A bright cloud overshadowed them, and from it the voice of the Father was heard (Matt. 17:1–5).

And on the fortieth day after His Resurrection, when Christ ascended from the Mount of Olives, “a cloud received Him out of their sight” (Acts 1:9). The same cloud shall appear again at His Second Coming: “Behold, He is coming with clouds, and every eye shall see Him, even those who pierced Him” (Rev. 1:7).

3. The Cloud as the Saints

The cloud is also an image of the saints, in whom the glory of God is revealed across the ages. St. Paul writes: “Since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily ensnares us” (Heb. 12:1).

Why are the saints likened to clouds? Just as the cloud shields us from the burning heat of the sun, so the saints, through their prayers, shield us from the wrath of God. Where there are clouds, there is rain; where there are saints, there is mercy. Their intercession brings refreshment to the Church as rain waters the earth.

4. The Virgin Mary as the Highest Cloud

Above all, the Virgin Mary is the cloud most glorious. In her, the Creator revealed His glory more profoundly than in any other creature. The prophets foretold her, Moses proclaimed her, and through her God made His dwelling among men. Her womb became His throne for nine months; from her flesh He took flesh, from her soul He took a soul, and at her breast He received nourishment. In her the glory of God was most perfectly revealed, hidden yet shining forth for the salvation of the world.

Conclusion

The cloud in Scripture is no ordinary vapor of the sky. It is the veil of divine majesty, the sign of God’s presence, the dwelling of His glory, the symbol of His saints, and the most perfect image of the Virgin Mother of God. Let us, therefore, look to the cloud not with earthly eyes, but with the eyes of faith, seeing in it the mercy, protection, and glory of the Lord who comes to save His people.

5139:
The Days and Times When #Prostration Is #Offered, and When It Is Not

(Part 6)

Beloved in Christ, today we learn when the Church commands us to bow down in repentance, and when She tells us to stand in joy. Prostration is holy, but it is not done at all times. For there is a season for sorrow and a season for gladness. Guided by Scripture and the canons of the Fathers, the Church shows us these proper times, so that our worship may be pleasing to God.

I. The Times When Prostration Is Forbidden

1. On Sundays

The first and chief among the days on which prostration is set aside is the Lord’s Day, the first day of the week, the day of His Resurrection. On this day we commemorate not mourning but victory, not abasement but triumph. For Christ, who was laid in the tomb, rose again in glory, and on this day He shall come again to judge the living and the dead.

The canons declare: “The known times when prostration to the ground is to be abandoned… are Sundays and the feast of Pentecost” (Fetha Negest, Article 14, No. 537). Again it says: “There is no prostration on Sundays and on the feasts of Pentecost, for these are days of joy” (Fetḥa Negest, Article 19, No. 715).
Thus the whole Church rejoices, standing upright before the Risen One, for the Sabbath of the new covenant is a day of liberty.

2. On Pentecost

Pentecost, the fiftieth day, is the feast of the Spirit, the day when heaven was opened and tongues of fire descended upon the apostles. It is the perfection of Pascha, the crown of fifty days of joy.
On this day, as the Fathers teach, fasting is abolished, and so also prostration. Even if the fiftieth day falls upon a Wednesday or Friday, days usually given to fasting, yet the feast prevails, and we eat and rejoice as on Christmas or Easter. 

3. On the Great Feasts of Our Lord

The law of the Church likewise forbids prostration on the great feasts of Christ. These are days of triumph, not lamentation. They include: His Conception, Nativity, Baptism, Hosanna, Resurrection, Ascension, Pentecost, and His Transfiguration on Mount Tabor. those are the eight feast of Christ but the Only one feast is excepted . the veneration of the Cross for though the Cross is an instrument of death, it is also the throne of His glory, and prostrate before it is .

4. On the Feast of Our Lady, the Theotokos

As the feasts of the Lord are days of joy, so also the feast of His holy Mother. The canons declare that on the days of her feast, prostration is not permitted. For she who bore the Word in her womb is honored in joy, not in mourning.

5. After Receiving Holy Eucharist 

Hear the wisdom of the Fathers: after partaking of the Body and Blood of Christ, we do not cast ourselves to the ground, but rather stand in reverence and thanksgiving, for the King of Glory has entered within us. The Fetha Negest says: “After receiving His body and blood, they refrain from worshipping” (Article 14, Nos. 536–537).

We do not abase ourselves, for He has lifted us up to communion with Himself. Our task in that hour is to glorify His Body and Blood, not to fall prostrate.

6. On the 12th, 21st, and 29th Days of Each Month

These days have been set aside by ancient custom.

The 12th is the feast of Saint Michael the Archangel, celebrated monthly in joy, for the Archangel is the defender of God’s people.

The 21st is dedicated to the Theotokos.

The 29th is consecrated to the memory of the Lord’s feasts.
On these days, as on the greater feasts, prostration is forbidden.

In addition to the nine major feasts of our Lord, there are also nine minor feasts. These include the Sermon, the Light, the Shepherd , the feast of Circumcision , Feast of the Presentation of the Lord, the Wedding at Cana of Galilee, the Mount of Olives, Gena, and the Feast of the Cross.

Although the King of Justice did not give a detailed explanation about these minor feasts, they are still counted as feasts of the Lord. Since prostration is forbidden on the feasts of the Lord, our forefathers treated these days in the same way. In particular, the 29th of the month was set apart as a feast of those 9 Minor feast , and on that day prostration is not performed.

In addition to the nine major and nine minor feasts, the Passion and the Resurrection are also counted among the feasts of the Lord.

The Church commands that the Passion be observed with prayer, fasting, and sorrow. The Resurrection, however, is celebrated differently. It begins on the day of Christ’s rising and continues throughout the week, until the feast known as the Second Resurrection.

Just as the Passion is remembered with mourning, fasting, and prayer, so also the Resurrection must be celebrated with fullness of joy. In the Passion we recall His crucifixion with devotion and sorrow, but in the Resurrection we rejoice in His victory over death.

Conclusion

See then, beloved, how wisely the Church instructs her children. She teaches us that there is a time to kneel and a time to stand, a time to weep and a time to rejoice. To prostrate on days of triumph would be to mingle grief with joy, but to stand upright on feast days is to confess the victory of Christ over death.

Therefore, let us honor the holy canons, and let our bodies be trained in obedience, as our souls are trained in faith. For discipline in outward worship shapes discipline in the inward man.

The Mystery of #Pagume, the Fast of #Yodit

Beloved in Christ, children of the Holy Church, grace and peace be multiplied to you from the Lord who renews the times and seasons, who gathers the years into His hand, and who makes the sun to rise over the righteous and the wicked alike. Today let us lift our minds to the holy mystery of Pagume, the voluntary fast of Judith, and the spiritual meaning hidden in this blessed season at the threshold of the New Year.


Pagume: The Increase of Days

The word Pagume means increase. It comes at the end of the Ethiopian year, and it is appointed for five days, or, once every four years in the leap year, for six days. Thus Ethiopia, in the providence of God, has earned the name: “The Land of Thirteen Months of Sunshine.”

When Pagume extends to six days, it aligns with the reckoning of the ancients, and in that year the fast of the Prophets, also called the fast of the Nativity, is broken on Nehase, with the celebration of the birth of Christ our Savior following thereafter.

The Voluntary Fast of (Yodit)

Among the two voluntary fasts preserved in the Holy Church, one belongs to this month of Pagume. It is called the Fast of (Yodit). Yet,beloved, many are unaware of this fast.

But let none confuse this holy Yodit with the infamous Yodit Gudit, the one remembered in church history for her destructive deeds. No, the Yodit whom we honor is she whom Scripture praises: a widow of Israel, a woman of courage, chastity, and fasting.

The Story of Yodit Victory

Hear the account, as the Holy Book records it:

When the mighty king Nebuchadnezzar had subdued his enemies, he sent forth his general Holofernes with twelve thousand foot soldiers and twelve thousand horsemen, saying, “Go, enlarge my dominion, receive tribute from the submissive, and crush those who resist” (Judith 2:7). With this command, Holofernes swept through many nations, destroying and subduing them, until he came to the land of Judah. There he inflicted great suffering, and the children of Israel cried out in anguish.

At that time, Judith(Yodit), whose husband had died, lived in holy widowhood. She dwelt apart, clothed herself in sackcloth, humbled her soul with fasting, and wept continually before God on behalf of her people. On the third day, as she entered the temple, the Lord who does not desire the ruin of His creation revealed to her the path of deliverance (Judith 8:2).

she Strengthened by prayer and fasting. Because of her, the Israelites rose up, pursued their enemies, and drove them as far as the Jordan. Thus was shame turned into victory, weakness into strength, mourning into triumph.

The Meaning of the Fast

Beloved, the Church therefore appoints this fast in the month of Pagume, so that we may imitate Judith’s holy zeal. For just as she conquered by fasting and prayer, so also must we, the children of the New Covenant, overcome our enemies: not flesh and blood, but Satan and the passions of the flesh.

Through voluntary fasting, we humble our bodies that our spirits may be exalted; we discipline our desires that we may receive power from the Creator; we arm ourselves with prayer that we may overcome the adversary.

Pagume and the Resurrection

Pagume also holds another mystery. It is the month of transition. As the year comes to its end, and as winter’s darkness prepares to pass, so Pagume reminds us of the greater passage: the Resurrection.

For just as Pagume turns us from the old year to the new, the Resurrection turns us from what is temporary to what is eternal, from earth to heaven, from death to life.

Every year, in the month of Pagume, Christians gather in the church from nightfall to receive baptism with holy water. Through this, we seek God’s mercy: that He may grant us a blessed new year, forgive the sins of the past, heal us from our infirmities, sanctify our lives, and prepare us for a future filled with His blessing.

A Prayer for the New Year

Let us then beseech the Lord of times and seasons:

That He grant us a new year of peace and health,

That He turn our hearts to repentance,

That He make us worthy to partake of His holy Body and precious Blood,

That He number us among the heirs of His everlasting Kingdom.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.

What does a #cloud #represent?”

(Part 3)

Beloved children of the covenant, heirs of the promise, and followers of the Orthodox faith, grace and peace be multiplied to you from God the Father and from our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Today we set before our hearts a sacred mystery: What is the symbol of the cloud? The Scriptures, the Fathers, and the holy tradition all testify to its meaning, showing us that the cloud is not a mere vapor of the sky but a living sign of God’s mercy, His covenant, and His dwelling among His people.

1. The Cloud of Noah – The Rainbow of the Covenant

After the great flood, when the waters had subsided and the ark came to rest, Noah, the righteous man, offered a sacrifice of thanksgiving. God, moved with mercy, blessed Noah and his sons, commanding them: “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth” (Gen. 9:1). Yet Noah, full of sorrow, spoke: “Lord, my children will sin again, and will You not in Your justice destroy them once more?”

Then the Lord, who is good and merciful, established a covenant of peace. He said: “I will set My bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth. Never again shall the waters become a flood to destroy all flesh” (Gen. 9:12–15). Thus, the rainbow appeared in the heavens as the seal of God’s promise.

The rainbow is not only a reminder that God will not flood the earth again it is also a symbol of Christ and His Mother, the Holy Virgin Mary. Just as the rainbow shines with four colors, for it is four-faced, symbolizing the flesh of man made from the four elements, and prefiguring the fullness of Christ revealed through the four holy Gospels. And as the rainbow rests in the cloud, so too the covenant of God rests in His chosen vessel, the Holy Virgin Mary.

Our Lord Jesus, while hanging on the cross, entrusted her to us, saying to the beloved disciple: “Behold your mother” (John 19:27). She is, therefore, the Mother of the Covenant. Just as the rainbow stood as a sign that the flood of wrath would not return, so the Virgin is the sign that salvation has come into the world through her Son.

The holy scholar Abba Giorgis, in his book Enzira Sibhat, praises her: “You are the rainbow of the covenant, the sign that the rain of wrath will no longer fall upon the earth.” Likewise, Abba Tsige and Abba Gebre Mariam in Mahlete Tsige proclaim: “The rainbow of Noah’s covenant is fulfilled in you, O Virgin, for as the heavens are adorned with stars, so the earth is adorned with flowers and fruits through you.” Thus, the cloud that bore the rainbow becomes a symbol of Mary, who bore the Sun of Righteousness, Christ Himself.

2. The Cloud of Moses – The Shelter of Mercy

Let us now look to the days of Moses, the great lawgiver. He led Israel out of bondage in Egypt into the wilderness. Yet the people hardened their hearts, grumbling and rebelling, so that the journey of forty days stretched into forty years. Among the rebels were Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. The earth opened and swallowed them, and judgment fell upon their households. Fear and confusion seized the people, and they rose against Moses and Aaron, crying out to stone them.

But what says the Scripture?

Scripture says: “Moses and Aaron went into the tabernacle of the congregation, and the cloud covered it, and the glory of the Lord appeared” (Num. 16:42). The cloud descended, wrapping them in God’s protection and saving them from destruction.

This cloud, too, is a symbol of the Holy Virgin Mary. Just as the cloud shielded Moses and Aaron, so the Virgin protects all who call upon her with faith. She is a refuge and a covering for those who trust in her, guarding them from the attacks of the enemy and interceding before her Son on their behalf.

Conclusion

Beloved, let us understand clearly: the cloud is a symbol of God’s covenant and His mercy. In the days of Noah, the cloud carried the rainbow, a promise of peace. In the days of Moses, the cloud covered the tabernacle, a sign of God’s protection. In both, the Holy Virgin Mary is revealed as the living cloud our Mother, our refuge, and our intercessor.

Therefore, let us glorify God who gave us such a sign, honor the Virgin who bore the Savior, and rejoice in the Cross by which we are redeemed.

What does a #cloud #represent?”

(Part 4)

Beloved brothers and sisters, today we continue learning about the mystery of the cloud in the Holy Scriptures. The cloud is not only a natural thing it is a sign chosen by God to reveal His covenant, His mercy, and His salvation. In this part, we look at the cloud of Elijah and the cloud of Isaiah.

3. The Cloud of Elijah – The Little Hand that Brought Rain

In the days of King Ahab, Israel was consumed with idolatry. The queen Jezebel slew the prophets of the Lord, raising up hundreds of false priests in their place. The king, instead of defending the worship of the true God, joined her in spreading corruption. Therefore, God’s servant Elijah, aflame with zeal, prayed that the heavens would be shut. And for three years and six months, no rain fell upon the earth; famine spread over the land, and the people suffered hunger.

When at last the time had come, God commanded Elijah to appear before Ahab. The prophet cried out: “How long will you hesitate between two opinions? If the Lord is God, follow Him!” (1 Kings 18:21). On Mount Carmel, before the priests of Baal and all the people, Elijah called upon the Lord, and fire descended from heaven to consume the sacrifice. The false prophets were silenced, and the God of Israel was glorified.

But the work of Elijah was not yet finished. He ascended Mount Carmel once more, bowed himself down, and prayed with his face between his knees. sent his servant to look toward the sea. The servant returned six times with nothing. But on the seventh time he said: “Behold, a little cloud, as small as a man’s hand, rises from the sea.” (1 Kings 18:44).

Then Elijah proclaimed: “Go, say to Ahab, prepare your chariot before the rain stops you!” And immediately, the sky grew black with clouds and wind, and a mighty rain fell, watering the earth and ending the famine (1 Kings 18:45).

Behold the mystery! The cloud was small, no larger than a man’s hand yet from it came a flood of rain that refreshed the land. So too the Holy Virgin Mary: though she appeared as a humble maiden among men, she was chosen to bear the Son of God. Through her, the true rain descended the mercy of Christ, the water of life, the comfort of those who hunger for peace and thirst for righteousness.

St. Ephrem the Syrian, in the hymns of the Church, praised her with these words: “You are the true cloud, O Virgin, from which descended the rain of mercy.”

4. The Cloud of Isaiah – The Swift Cloud Bearing the Lord

Seven centuries before the coming of Christ, the prophet Isaiah foresaw the mystery and declared: “Behold, the Lord rides upon a swift cloud, and shall come into Egypt” (Isaiah 19:1). Who is this swift cloud? The Fathers teach with one voice: it is the Holy Virgin Mary.

For when the Lord was born in Bethlehem, Herod sought to kill Him. An angel appeared to Joseph in a dream and commanded: “Take the young Child and His mother, and flee into Egypt” (Matthew 2:13). Thus was the prophecy fulfilled: the Lord indeed came into Egypt riding upon the cloud of His Mother. Through her, He entered into the land of idols and scattered their images, proving Himself to be the one true God.

Conclusion

Beloved, let us understand with fear and joy: the cloud in Scripture always points us to the same mystery. To Noah, the cloud bore the rainbow of the covenant. To Moses, it covered the tabernacle with God’s glory. To Elijah, it appeared as a small hand bringing rain. To Isaiah, it was the swift cloud carrying the Lord into Egypt.

In all these, the cloud reveals the Holy Virgin Mary. She is the cloud who bore the Sun of Righteousness, the hand through which the mercy of God was poured, the vessel chosen to carry the Savior into the world. Through her, the famine of sin is ended, and the drought of mercy is filled with abundant rain.

Therefore, let us cry out with faith: “O Virgin Mary, our covenant and our cloud, remember us before your Son!”

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always.

The Mystery of the Month of #Pagume, #Fasting, and #Baptism

Beloved in Christ, today we reflect on the deep meaning of the month of Pagume and the wisdom of the Church in teaching us to fast and to seek baptism during these holy days. May God’s grace, the prayers of the saints, and the protection of His holy angels guide and strengthen us.

The Mystery of Pagume

Pagume is unlike the other months. In the order of the Ethiopian calendar it stands as the thirteenth month, short in days but great in meaning. It has either five days or, in the years of St. John, six days. Pagume Three , in this time the seven heavens are opened and the prayers of the faithful ascend unhindered before the throne of God.

Though small in number of days, its greatness surpasses many months, for it symbolizes a transition. Just as the year passes from old into new, so Pagume proclaims the mystery of the end of the world: a passage from time to eternity, from the temporal life to the everlasting kingdom, from the darkness of winter to the dawn of unending day. Thus, it becomes for us an image of the Day of Judgment, when Christ shall appear in glory to judge the living and the dead.

Why Do We Fast in Pagume?

Because Pagume is a remembrance of the last day, the Church teaches us to pass through it with fasting, prayer, and supplication. Monks in monasteries spend these days as in a closed week of devotion, shutting out the noise of the world.

This fasting is not one of compulsion, for Pagume is not counted among the seven great fasts of the Church. Yet the faithful, desiring the blessings of God, willingly embrace it. For if we sanctify the eve of the New Year with prayer and humility, the year to come will be filled with blessings according to the will of God.

Our fathers have shown us the path: with fasting, they prayed for the good of the nation, for the peace of the Church, for the mercy of the Creator. And we, their children, must imitate them. If we spend Pagume not in feasting or drunkenness but in fasting, God will reconcile us, heal our wounds, destroy pestilence, and grant unity and peace to His Holy Church and to our land.

Why Are We Baptized in Pagume?

Many believers are baptized in Pagume because this month is connected to the Archangel Raphael, whose name means “God heals.”

During Pagume, the waters of the world rivers, seas, lakes, and even rain are blessed by angels.

Because of this, baptism in these waters brings healing from sickness and protection from evil.

Farmers also believe that even their crops are purified during Pagume, especially on Pagume 3rd, which is the feast day of Archangel Raphael.

The Bible confirms this mystery: “For at certain times an angel of the Lord went down into the pool and stirred the water; and whoever stepped in first was healed of whatever disease he had” (John 5:4). In the same way, during Pagume, the Archangel Raphael blesses the waters for healing and salvation.

On Pagume 3rd:

Rain that falls is collected and kept as holy water.

It is sprinkled in homes, soaked into grain, and given to the sick, because it drives away evil spirits and brings blessing.

Pregnant women may drink from this water, because Raphael is called the opener of the womb, and by God’s mercy he helps them give birth safely.

Raphael Among the Angels

Raphael is one of the seven princes who stand before the throne of God. As he himself declared in the Book of Tobit: “I am Raphael, one of the seven princes of glory” (Tobit 12:15). In the beginning, when God created the angelic hosts, He placed Raphael over many tribes of angels, and in Ramah he established him as leader of the mighty ones. Thus, he is not only a healer of men but a commander of angels, ever ready to serve the will of the Most High.

Pagume and the Second Coming

Finally, Pagume calls to our remembrance the return of Christ. In the hymns of the Church, sung during these days, we proclaim His coming in majesty, His judgment of the nations, and the establishment of the new age. The shortness of this month reminds us that time itself will come to an end, and that eternity will soon begin.

Thus, every day of Pagume is a summons to repentance, a call to purity, a preparation for the Lord who is to come.

Conclusion

Beloved, let us not spend these days in vain indulgence but in sober watchfulness. Let us fast with sincerity, pray with faith, and if possible, partake in the mystery of baptism with holy water blessed by the Archangel Raphael. Then, reconciled to God, we shall receive healing for body and soul, peace for our homes, and blessings for the year ahead.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

5160:
The #Sea of #Thoughts(#Bahre #ḥasāb) and the Sage Who Reached It

(Part 1)

Beloved children of the Orthodox faith, grace and peace be multiplied to you. Today let us reflect on a mystery handed down in the Church, a subject both profound and wondrous: the Sea of Thoughts what it means, and who is the blessed sage that attained its depth. May the Holy Spirit enlighten us as we consider this teaching.

What Is the Sea of Thoughts?

The Sea of Thoughts is a name given to the ordered measure of time, a numbered era. It is called a sea because of its vastness and depth, just as the waters of the ocean spread out beyond sight. In the same way, the Sea of Thoughts includes not only the simple counting of numbers addition, subtraction, multiplication to fix the days of feasts and fasts, but also the contemplation of the sun, the moon, and the stars.

For time itself is not random, but is arranged by God and entrusted to the stewardship of the Church. Humanity, in obedience to divine wisdom, arranges the divisions of days, months, and years so that both social life and the worship of God may proceed in order.

The Science of Time

This holy science of measuring time is called Bahre ḥasāb. The word is joined from two parts:

Bahir — meaning time or period.

Ḥasābe — meaning counting, reckoning, or measure.


Thus Bahre ḥasāb signifies a numbered period or world-year.

It is likened to the sea because of its vastness: its depths contain secrets upon secrets, hidden meanings and mysteries, just as the ocean has unfathomable paths. In this way, the reckoning of times is not merely practical but spiritual it reveals the order of God’s creation and guides His people in their worship.

The Sea of Thoughts in the Church’s Library

The wisdom of the Sea of Thoughts is preserved within the treasury of the Church. Our spiritual library is founded upon four councils or pillars:

1. The Old Testament

2. The New Testament

3. The Book of the Monks

4. The Elders (Haymanote Abew)

And beyond these is a Fifth Council, which is divided into two ways: the path of Abu Shakar and the path of the Sea of Thoughts itself.

This shows that the Sea of Thoughts belongs within the very heart of the Church’s teaching authority it is no invention of man, but part of the wisdom guarded by the Fathers.

The Sage Who Reached the Sea of Thoughts

Many holy men desired to enter this sea, but only by the will of God was it revealed. The one chosen was Saint Demetrius, the twelfth bishop of Alexandria.

In his youth he was a simple man, devoted to agricultural work, with no reputation for scholarship. Yet God, who exalts the humble and confounds the proud, filled him with the Holy Spirit and opened to him the mysteries of the times.

Thus it was through Demetrius that the Church received the system of timekeeping, the calendar by which the feasts and fasts have been ordered for centuries.

The Meaning of Demetrius’ Name

The name Demetrius is full of mystery. It means mirror. Just as a mirror reflects what is hidden from the eye, so Saint Demetrius revealed to the Church the hidden feasts and the hidden order of time.

A mirror shows what is far away so Demetrius made clear what was distant and unseen.

A mirror shows what is subtle and fine so Demetrius brought to light what was delicate and concealed.

A mirror shows what is scattered so Demetrius gathered together the mysteries of time into one clear vision.

For this reason the Fathers called him a mirror, for through him God revealed the concealed treasures of His calendar.

Conclusion

Behold then, beloved, the Sea of Thoughts: vast, deep, and mysterious, a reflection of God’s eternal order. And behold the sage, Saint Demetrius of Alexandria, who by the grace of the Holy Spirit reached its depths and gave to the Church the gift of time’s reckoning.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

The Feast of the Archangel Saint #Raphael (#Pagume 3)

Beloved in Christ, children of the holy Church, peace and grace be multiplied unto you. Today we gather to remember with reverence the annual feast of the Archangel Raphael, which shines forth on the third day of Pagume. Among the many commemorations of this blessed month, this feast holds a special place, for it calls us to contemplate the mercy of God revealed through His angelic minister, Raphael, whose very name proclaims: “Healing from God.”

The Name and Dignity of Raphael

The name Raphael comes from two words: Rufa, meaning health, medicine, and healing, and El, the holy name of God. Joined together, the name declares his mission: healing given by God to His people. Thus the Lord testified in the Scripture: “Behold, I send My angel before you… Do not resist him, for My name is in him” (Ex. 23:20–22).

This Raphael, the gentle and merciful one, stands among the seven archangels, and in rank is placed after Michael and Gabriel. Of himself he bore witness, saying: “I am Raphael, one of the seven chiefs who bring the prayers of the saints before the throne of glory” (Tobit 12:15).

He is, therefore, both intercessor and guardian, offering our supplications to God, reconciling us to the Creator, and ever praising the Most High with the heavenly hosts.

The Sevenfold Ministry of Raphael

1. The Healer of the Sick "Fewase Duyan"

When our Lord Jesus Christ walked the earth, He healed both body and soul. Likewise, Raphael has been appointed by the Almighty to heal mankind of sickness and of sin. Enoch testifies: “Saint Raphael is appointed over all diseases and wounds of the children of men” (Enoch 10:13).

Thus, as Christ healed the paralytic with the words “Rise, take up your bed, and walk” (Jn. 5:8), so Raphael heals by intercession and prayer, curing wounds both visible and hidden. He is a physician of God, a protector who shields us from the maladies of flesh and the corruption of the soul.

2. The Opener of the Womb"Fetahe Mahtsen"

God, who made barren Sarah to laugh with joy, who gave children to Rachel, Hannah, and Elizabeth, has appointed Raphael as minister of this mystery. He comforts mothers in labor, protects children in the womb, and eases the pangs of childbirth.

From the first moment of conception until the hour of delivery, Raphael does not depart, but stands guard as a heavenly midwife, easing pain and safeguarding life. Thus mothers cry his name in prayer, and through his intercession are delivered with joy.

3. The Exorcist of Demons"Sadade Aganant"

As Christ cast out unclean spirits, so Raphael has received authority to bind the demons. When Sarah, daughter of Raguel, was tormented by the demon Asmodeus, Raphael expelled him with divine power (Tobit 3:8, 17).

Enoch also records: “Bind Azazel hand and foot, and cast him into the darkness” (Enoch 10:4–7). This same Raphael is today sent to drive away from us envy, hatred, deceit, and every whisper of the evil one.

4. The Advocate of Prayer"Akabe Hohat"

Raphael is not only healer and protector, but also intercessor, who carries the prayers of men before the throne of God. As he declared: “I am Raphael… who brings the prayers of the saints before the glory of the Holy One” (Tobit 12:15).

A wondrous miracle bears witness: when the faithful prayed in a church on an island near Alexandria, the devil sought to destroy them by stirring the waters beneath. Yet when they cried out to God in Raphael’s name, the angel struck the reef with the sign of the Cross, and the danger ceased. Thus he revealed himself as guardian of the faithful and protector of the Church.

5. The Guide of the Way (Meraë Fênot)

When young Tobias journeyed to Media, Raphael went with him in the form of a companion, guiding and protecting him from dangers (cf. Ex. 23:20). At the river Tigris, when a great fish sought to swallow him, Raphael delivered him and showed him how its gall and liver would become medicine and weapon against evil.

Thus is Raphael revealed as guide to travelers, protector of pilgrims, and helper to those who face trials along the road. Even now, the Church invokes him as guardian of the way.

6. The Angel of Marriage"Melake Kebkab"

Raphael is also called the Angel of the Bridegroom, for he blessed the union of Tobias and Sarah. Though Sarah’s seven husbands had perished by the demon’s hand, Raphael taught Tobias how to overcome the evil one: by prayer, by faith, and by the burning of the fish’s liver.

That night, the demon fled, and Tobias and Sarah prayed together, committing their marriage to God. As Christ blessed the wedding at Cana, so Raphael sanctified theirs, showing that true marriage is preserved not by fleshly desire, but by the fear of God and the intercession of His saints.

Even now, Raphael blesses the marriages of the faithful, making their homes secure in peace.

7. The Enlightener of the Blind "Kesate Eweran"

Finally, Raphael restored the sight of Tobit, father of Tobias, by means of the fish’s gall. Just as Christ opened the eyes of the blind with clay and spittle, so Raphael gave light to Tobit’s darkness.

Thus he is the angel who enlightens not only the eyes of the body, but the eyes of the heart. He opens for us the vision of faith, that we may behold the mercy of God and walk in His light.

The Feast of Pagume 3

Beloved, this feast falls in the month of Pagume, which is the bridge between the old year and the new. The Fathers teach us that Pagume signifies the Day of Resurrection: the cleansing of the old age, and the preparation for the Kingdom of God to come.

Thus the feast of Raphael, celebrated on Pagume 3, is the crown of the passing year and the threshold of the new. The waters of this time are believed to be blessed, and the faithful cry out in faith: “Saint Raphael, help us! Protect us!”

How is the #Time System Defined in #Ethiopia? 

(Part 2)

Beloved in Christ, sons and daughters of the holy Orthodox faith, we greet you with the peace of God. Today we turn our attention to the mystery of time as it is ordered in Ethiopia a land sanctified by the Gospel, whose very measure of days bears witness to the wisdom of the Creator. Let us therefore behold with reverence how the year is divided, how the seasons are appointed, and how the order of months gives glory to God, who is the Lord of times and ages.

1. The Ethiopian Year and Its Seasons

The Ethiopian reckoning of time is wondrous and full of meaning. Unlike the systems of other nations, Ethiopia counts a year as consisting of thirteen months, and it is divided into four great seasons. These are not arbitrary, but carefully set in order by divine providence and witnessed to in the writings of Saint Yared.

The four seasons are:

1. Keremt – from Sene 26 to Meskerem 25.

2. Metsew (Tbi) – from Meskerem 26 to Tahisas 25.

3. Bega (Hagay) – from Tahisas 26 to Megabit 25.

4. Tsedey – from Megabit 26 to Sene 25.

Each season has 99 days, except Keremt, which has 95 days.

Saint Yared, the holy hymnographer, spoke of these seasons and showed how each one gives glory to God.

2. The Four Seasons in Detail

2.1 The Season of Metsew (Tbi)

This season, also called Tbi, begins in the fourth week after Keremt. It runs from Meskerem 26 to Tahisas 25, making 90 days in total.

Saint Yared gives it a noble description: “You made the seasons so that we may boast of your wonderful power. You gave the Keremt for rain and the Metsew for flowers” (Digwa Zetsge Kufale 2 Jo.2÷23; cf. Jer. 5:24).

This is the season of harvest. The rains of Keremt water the earth, and in Metsew the earth brings forth fruit in abundance. Flowers bloom across Ethiopia on fields, hills, and mountains alike. Its chief months are Tikimt, Hidar, and Tahisas. It is truly the time of nature’s adornment, when the earth rejoices in her Creator.

2.2. The Season of Bega (Haggay)

Following Metsew comes Bega, also called Hagay, which stretches from Tahisas 26 to Megabit 25, encompassing the months of Tir, Yekatit, and Megabit.

The word Hagay is derived from the Geʿez tongue, meaning “summer” or “time of the sun.” One fourth of the year it occupies, and thus it is called the hand of the seasons. Scripture itself acknowledges this order: “You made Keremt and Bega” (Ps. 75:17; Zech. 14:10; Gen. 10:22).

Bega is the season of brightness, of harvest, of spring and dryness. The grains, ripened by the sun, are gathered into barns. In this time, Ethiopia celebrates the fruit of labor. Yekatit, in particular, is a month when the gathered harvest is safely stored. Because the barns are full, the people turn to feasting, celebrating baptisms, marriages, and annual festivals. This period is known as the Merawi, the season of rejoicing.

2.3. The Season of Tsedey

Next comes Tsedey, a season of transition, stretching from Megabit 26 to Sene 25. It includes the months of Miyaziya, Ginbot, and Sene.

Tsedey contains the qualities of the other seasons. On one hand, it is the time of the Belig harvest—sown, reaped, and threshed. On the other, it is the time when the land is prepared for the coming Keremt rains. Thus, it is both the season of conclusion and of preparation.

Saint Yared in his hymn declares."ይሁብ ዝናመ ተወን"(yihub zname tewen)  the Belg rains are given.” The people labor diligently, sowing where there is fall rain, and where there is none, plowing and preparing the fields. An old proverb says, “One Sene does not replace two Sene that are harvested,” reminding us that diligence today cannot be postponed to tomorrow.

2.4 The Season of Keremt

Keremt, from Sene 26 to Meskerem 25, is the season of rain and water. Its months are Hamle, Nehase, Pagume, and Meskerem. Water, in this season, pours forth from heaven, washing the earth, quenching its fire, and blessing it with moisture.

Saint Yared declares:The Lord of the Ages, the Almighty, brings us winter every year, and the clouds hear His word.” The rains of Keremt are not mere waters, but the mercy and blessing of God poured upon His people. It is the season of renewal and life-giving abundance, when the earth, like a servant, listens to the word of its Master.

3. The Year of the Evangelists

The years of John, Matthew, and Mark are 365 days and 6 hours (from Meskerem 1 to Pagume 5).

The year of Luke alone is 366 days (from Meskerem 1 to Pagume 6).

Thus, the four Evangelists themselves mark the rhythm of the year, binding time to the Gospel.


4. The Months of the Year

The word for month in Geʿez is Werh, which in Amharic is Werh and in plural form Wereh. In the Ethiopian calendar, there are twelve months of thirty days each. At the end, five days are added or six in the leap year of Luke. This differs from the Western system, where months vary in length.

Unlike the European calendar, the months are equal in length, reflecting order and balance.

Conclusion

Thus, beloved, the Ethiopian reckoning of time is no mere human invention but a reflection of divine wisdom. It marks the turning of the seasons with prayer, labor, and thanksgiving. Each season carries its own mystery: Keremt brings rain, Metsew brings flowers, Bega brings harvest and joy, Tsedey brings diligence and preparation.

As Saint Yared and the Scriptures testify, God Himself ordains the times and the seasons, that man may remember His power and give thanks. Truly, time itself becomes a hymn to the Creator: the rains, the sun, the harvest, and the plow all sing the praises of the Lord who gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater.

May the name of the Holy God be praised forever and ever in every tongue that He has created, today and always. 

May the blessings of God's mother, the virgin, and the cross be upon us.
Amen.

Brethren beloved in Christ, let us behold the mystery of time, not as a mere counting of hours, but as the wisdom of God written upon creation. For He who set the sun to rule the day and the moon the night has also appointed the months and the years, that man might learn to order his life in holiness. The Ethiopian reckoning of time is not invention of men alone, but a heritage sanctified by labor, by memory, and by faith.

1. The Months and Their Origins in Ge’ez

The year of Ethiopia, preserved in the tongue of the fathers, Ge’ez, is not a mere calendar of convenience, but a mirror of life, labor, and the mysteries of God’s providence. Each month bears a name not chosen at random, but springing from the rhythms of creation and the deeds of man.

Meskerem (1st month) — From Mes’e and Kerem, meaning “the night has passed, the rainy season is over.” Just as Noah beheld the dry land after the flood, so too Meskerem proclaims new beginnings after the darkness of rain.

Tikimt (2nd month) — From "Tekeme", meaning “work, useful time.” This month summons us to diligence, reminding us that man was placed in the garden to labor and keep it.

Hidar (3rd month) — From "Hadere," “to spend the night in the harvest field.” It recalls the toil and vigilance of the farmer, who guards his fruits even through the night.

Tahsas (4th month) — From "Hasese", meaning “searched.” In this month crops are inspected, and the fathers teach that it also signifies the searching of the wise men who sought the newborn Christ. Thus, it binds earthly labor to divine revelation.

Tir (5th month) — From Netere, Teyere, Atreye, meaning “flash, heat, buying season.” The sun burns, and commerce is busy, cattle and grain exchanged. Creation teaches man both need and provision.

Yekatit (6th month) — From Ketete, Ketit, “to nest, to store in the barn.” 

Megabit (7th month) — From "Megebe", “to feed, to eat standing.” A month of strength and nourishment, calling man to rise and be sustained.

Miyazya (8th month) — From "Mehaze", “to be brave, to be strong,” and also remembered as the season of weddings. It binds together courage and joy, the household and the covenant.

Ginbot (9th month) — From "Genebe", “to build, to dig, to prepare the land.” Here we see the farmer clearing fields, just as the soul must prepare its heart for the seed of the Word.

Sene (10th month) — From "Seneye", “beautiful.” Nature itself bursts into glory, creation testifying to the majesty of God.

Hamle (11th month) — From "Hamele", “to harvest, to pick.” The barns are filled, but let us not forget the greater harvest, when the Lord of the vineyard shall return for His fruit.

Nehase (12th month) — From Anahsye, Nehase, “to lighten, to ease.” The heavy rains depart, and the earth breathes relief. 

Pagume (13th month) — From the Greek Epagumenos, “to add.” It is an addition, a reminder that God’s times are not bound by man, but that He adds as He wills.

Thus each month is a sermon in itself, and a chapter of creation.

👉Tir: Day length 10 hours Night length 14 hours

👉Yekatit: Day length 11 hours Night length 13 hours

👉Megabit: Day length 12 hours Night length 12 hours

👉Miyazya: Day length 13 hours Night length 11 hours

👉Ginbot: Day length 14 hours Night length 10 hours

👉Sene: Day length 15 hours Night length 09 hours

👉Hamle: Day length 14 hours Night length 10 hours

👉Nehase: Day length 13 hours, the length of the night is 11 hours.

So the cycle of day and night preaches to us the mysteries of life: there is a time of joy and a time of trial, a time when light seems hidden and a time when it shines in glory. Yet all is measured by the wisdom of Him who “made the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night” (Genesis 1:16).

3. The Week and the Days

Time is further bound in the cycle of the week, called Samint, from the Ge’ez word Semene meaning “eight.” For though the week has seven days, the cycle leads us from Sunday back to Sunday, from first to first, thus creating an eighth day that foreshadows eternity — the day beyond time, the Day of the Lord.

Each day bears its meaning from creation itself:

Sunday (Ehud) — From Ahade, “to make one.” It is the first day, the day when God began His creation.

Monday (Segno) — From Saneye, “to make two.” It marks the second day, when God divided the waters above and below.

Tuesday (Maksegno / Selus) — From Selese, “to make three.” The third day, when the earth brought forth vegetation.

Wednesday (E'rob) — From Rebi’a, “to make four.” The day when the heavenly lights were set in their place.

Saturday (Kidame )" Kedamit"— Meaning “first,” for it is the first Sabbath, the day of holy rest, when God sanctified the seventh day.

Thus, the very names of the days are a living catechism of creation, teaching us each week to remember the mighty works of God.

Each month, each day, each hour whispers the voice of God: “Redeem the time, for the days are evil” (Ephesians 5:16). 5178:
How is the Time #System Defined in #Ethiopia?

(Part 4)

Beloved children of the Church, heirs of the ancient faith of the fathers, peace and grace be multiplied unto you. Today we turn to a matter profound and wondrous: the understanding of time itself, and how our Ethiopian tradition preserved through the wisdom of the saints and scholars defines, measures, and sanctifies it.

For time is no mere invention of men, but a gift from God, a framework within which the mystery of salvation unfolds. As the Psalmist testifies: “Of old Thou didst lay the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the work of Thy hands. They shall perish, but Thou shalt endure; yea, all of them shall wax old like a garment, and as a vesture shalt Thou change them, and they shall be changed. But Thou art the same, and Thy years shall have no end” (Ps. 101:24–28).

Thus, while the heavens and the earth pass away, the Lord remains immutable; and man, His creature, moves through the appointed times until he returns to the Maker.

The Scholar of Time: Abushakhr Wolde Abel Herem

The Scholar of Time: Abushakhr Wolde Abel Herem

Among those who reflected on the divine order of times was Abushakhr Wolde Abel Herem, also remembered as Yohannes Fiqrum. He was a mathematician and philosopher, one who delved into the mystery of chronology and the reckoning of days. His work, published in 1962, builds upon the study of ancient systems of time.

Nine scholars,  examined and commented on his numbers and ideas:

Seid Welde Bettrik

Mahboub Menbegawi

Seidawyan  Jews

Yohannes Afewerk

Qerlos

Epiphanios

Yohannes Zedamasko

Markos Welde Qember

Giorgis Welde Amid (also called Hamid)

Though his book is mathematical, Ethiopians also count it as a poetic book, because it explains time in a way that praises God’s creation.

The Threefold Division of Time

Abushakhr explains that time, when measured by the conscience, divides itself into three great periods:

1. The time of the present – that which we see and live in.

2. The time of the past – that which has been and is remembered.

3. The time of the prophet (the future) – that which is yet to come and is foretold.

Thus, human thought, word, and action are bound in time. Our life is measured in ages, our deeds unfold in succession, and our salvation is worked out in the history God governs.

Moses himself, speaking in Deuteronomy, bears witness to this mystery: “Since the day that God created man upon the earth, and from one end of heaven unto the other, hath there been any such thing as this great thing is, or hath been heard like it?” (Deut. 4:32).

The Year of the World

The Ethiopian system teaches that from Adam to Christ there are 5,500 years. This is called the Year of Judgment (Fda). From the birth of Christ until now, we live in the Year of Mercy, the age of grace brought forth by the Incarnation.

The union of these two gives us the Year of the World (Amete Alem):

Year of the World = Year of Mercy + Year of Judgment

Thus, in the year 2018 A.D., the calculation is:

2018 + 5500 = 7518

The Evangelical Cycle

Time is also sanctified through the witness of the Four Evangelists. The Year of the World is divided by four, revealing which Gospel governs the age.

2018 + 5500 = 7518

7518 ÷ 4 = 1879 {remainder 2}

7518 - ( 4 × 1879)

         = 7518 -  7516=2

If remainder = 1 → the time of Matthew

If remainder = 2 → the time of Mark

If remainder = 3 → the time of Luke

If remainder = 0 → the time of John

Thus, since the remainder is 2, the year 2018 belongs to Mark, the Evangelist of boldness and action. This is the Time of Mark.

Even if we divide only the Year of Mercy (2018) by four, the result is the same: remainder 2 again, the time of Mark.

Beloved in Christ, children of the Holy Church, grace and peace be to you. The fathers of the Church teach that the reason Ethiopia celebrates the New Year in Meskerem is that the sun, the moon, and the stars complete their yearly cycle in the small month of Pagumē and begin anew in "Meskerem". At this sacred turning, day and night are equal, each being twelve hours, just as in the beginning when God created balance and order.

The year, carefully counted, has 364 days, and thus the transition into Meskerem marks the fullness of creation’s cycle.

If remainder is 3, it is the time of Luke.

If no remainder, it is the time of John.

In this way, time itself is joined to the preaching of the Gospel, and every year is sanctified under the voice of an Evangelist.

A Lesson on #Saint #John (ርዕሰ አውድ ዓመት)

Beloved children of the Orthodox faith, peace and grace be multiplied to you in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Today we turn our hearts to the mystery of Saint John (R-E'se Awdamet), the day that crowns the beginning of the Ethiopian year and fills the faithful with joy and repentance.

1. The Meaning of the Name “John”

The name John means “Grace of God.” This is not a small matter, for the grace of God is the fountain of all life, the root of forgiveness, and the power by which sinners are made saints. Just as the Scriptures tell us of John the Baptist he was sent ahead of Christ, proclaiming repentance so the very name testifies that God’s grace is given to humanity through him.

2. The Universal Commemoration of John

The Church, guided by divine wisdom, commemorates Saint John in the times of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Before the year begins, he is remembered. Why? Because John is the one who stands at the threshold of two covenants: at the end of the Old Testament and at the dawn of the New. He is the lamp shining before the Sun of Righteousness.

3. John the Baptist in Scripture

Saint Mark, echoing Isaiah, says: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare the way of the Lord, make His paths straight” (Mark 1:1–4; Isaiah 40:3–4). This voice was none other than John the Baptist, son of Zechariah, who baptized in the wilderness, who bore witness to Christ, and who announced salvation by repentance and forgiveness. His ministry was not for himself, but for the Lord whom he proclaimed.

4. Why the Year Begins with John

When the fathers of the Church established the order of feasts, they decreed that the first day of Meskerem the first day of the Ethiopian year be dedicated to Saint John. Thus, every year begins with his memory, for he is the gateway of the Gospel, and his ministry marks the turning of ages. The (Dirsane Ze kidus Yohannes Afewerq) testifies that our fathers wisely set this rule for the Church.

5. The Biblical Foundation of the New Year

The Book of Numbers teaches that the beginning of the year in Meskerem is a blessed season. On this day, the hours of day and night are equal twelve and twelve. After this day, the daylight begins to decrease. The change of the seasons, marked by the stars, the sun, and the moon, is not by accident but by divine order. As the book of Enoch declares: “He created the sun and the moon as a sign of the time” (Enoch 21:49).

Even in the time of Noah, it was in the first month that the waters subsided, and the earth appeared again (Genesis 8:13). Thus, the rebirth of the world after the flood coincided with this sacred month. The fathers saw in this the historical and divine root of the New Year: a new creation, a new beginning, a fresh grace.

6. The Spiritual Call of the New Year

The feast of Saint John, or R-ʾEse Awdamet, is not only about days and numbers. It is a call to repentance and renewal. As Saint Paul teaches: “Behold, the old things have passed away, and all things are become new in Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:17). On this day, we are urged to leave behind evil deeds, and to clothe ourselves with new good works that please God.

The fathers compare this to:

a student advancing to a higher level,

a farmer planting after the winter,

a worker persevering through rains to see the summer sun.

So too the faithful must embrace spiritual growth as the new year dawns.

7. Enkutatash – The Pearl of the New Year

This feast is also called Enkutatash, meaning “the gift of jewels.” Two ancient traditions explain this:

In the time of Noah, When Noah first divided the continents among his three sons, Africa was given to Cam.he landed in Ethiopia during Meskerem. Seeing the land blooming with beauty, he cried and said “You have given me a pearl of a pearl!”(Enku Eta wetashlgn  ) Hence, this season was named Enkutatash.

In the time of the Queen of Sheba, when she visited Solomon, she brought rich gifts of gold and spices. Solomon, showing her the treasures of his palace, placed a jewel upon her finger, saying: “Let the pearl be an ornament for you.” This also took place in Meskerem, and from it the name Enkutatash entered our heritage.

Thus, Enkutatash signifies joy, blessing, and the flowering of new life.

8. The Duty of the Present Generation

For more than two thousand years, the Ethiopian Church has preserved the good works and borne the trials of the generations. Now it is our turn. We must strengthen monasteries, promote the spread of the Gospel, build good administration, and preserve unity with sister churches. Faith is not a heritage to be wasted, but a treasure to be safeguarded and handed down.

9. Conclusion – A Call to Repentance and Fruitfulness

Beloved, the feast of Saint John is not a mere tradition. It is the voice of repentance at the gateway of every year. It is the trumpet calling us to turn away from sin and to begin anew with God. May the Lord grant us in this year to return with repentance, to bear fruit thirty, sixty, and a hundredfold, and to inherit the Kingdom prepared for His saints.

Amen.
